title: Abuse Safeguarding
description: Equip every worker to recognise the signs of abuse and neglect, respond safely in the moment, and report through the provider's system and to the NDIS Commission where required.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; NDIS Code of Conduct

steps.title: What abuse and neglect look like
paragraphs: Abuse is harm done to a person. Physical abuse includes hitting, pushing, rough handling, and force used to get a task done. Sexual abuse is any sexual act, exposure, or comment without free consent, including where the person cannot consent. Emotional and psychological abuse is threats, humiliation, isolation, or constant criticism that wears someone down. Financial abuse and exploitation is taking money, property, or benefits, or pressuring someone to hand them over.

Neglect is care that does not happen. Active neglect is refusing care you know the person needs. Passive neglect is not noticing that they have not eaten, been changed, or had their medication. Discrimination and systemic abuse is when rules, routines, or attitudes treat a person as less, or shut them out of ordinary life. You notice harm through the body (injuries, pain, weight loss), through behaviour (fear, withdrawal, a new sexualised act), and through the place (no food, a locked room, missing belongings).
points: Physical, sexual, emotional and psychological abuse

steps.title: Why risk is higher
paragraphs: People who rely on others for personal care, meals, money, or communication have less room to protect themselves. A person who needs you to get out of bed cannot easily leave a shift that feels wrong. If they communicate in ways other people dismiss, a disclosure can be written off as confusion or behaviour. That is why you take what they show you seriously the first time.

Risk rises in closed settings: a house with few visitors, a shift with one worker, a van, a bedroom with the door shut. Isolation means fewer people see what happens. There is also a power difference on every shift. You know the system, you can leave at the end of the shift, and you are often physically stronger. They live with the consequences. You use that difference to protect them, never to get your own way.
points: Power imbalance between worker and participant

steps.title: Recognising it in practice
paragraphs: Watch for change, not a textbook picture. A person may become withdrawn, angry, or frightened of a particular worker. Money or belongings go missing. They stop wanting to go somewhere they used to enjoy. Injuries they cannot explain, or an explanation that changes each time you ask, need a closer look. Bruises in different stages of healing, marks that match a hand or a strap, and pain during personal care are physical signs.

Also watch other workers. A colleague who insists on working alone with someone, who mocks them, who takes them to the bank, or who is secretive about a shift is a warning. Grooming is a pattern: gifts, secrets, special treatment, slowly crossing a physical boundary, and isolating the person from family or other staff. One kind act is not grooming. A pattern that builds secrecy and dependence is. You do not need proof. You report what you noticed.
points: Changes in behaviour, mood, money or belongings
Grooming behaviour by adults toward participants

steps.title: Responding to a disclosure
paragraphs: If someone tells you they have been hurt, listen and believe them enough to act. You do not interview them, ask leading questions, or make them repeat the story for each new person. Your job is safety, not the investigation. Meet immediate medical needs first. If they are injured, bleeding, or in pain, get health care. If they are unsafe with a person who is still there, separate them.

Say you are glad they told you, that they are not in trouble, and that you will get help. Do not promise secrecy. You will have to tell the people whose job it is to protect them. Leave clothing, bedding, and the place as they are when you can do that without leaving the person unsafe. Do not confront the person they named. Confrontation can silence them, destroy evidence, and put you both at risk. Write down the words they used, as soon as you can, and report.
points: What to say and what not to promise
Preserving evidence; not confronting the alleged person

steps.title: Reporting
paragraphs: Tell your provider through the incident pathway the same shift, not at the end of the week. Say what you saw or were told, who was there, and what you did. Do not wait to be sure. The people who assess the report decide what happens next. If a child is involved, police and the child-protection report in your state may be required as well as the internal report. Do that immediately. Do not agree to 'keep it in the house'.

Some events are reportable to the NDIS Commission. Death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact, and sexual misconduct are reported within 24 hours. You tell your provider so they can make that notification. You are protected when you report in good faith. Retaliation for raising a safety concern is itself a breach. If you fear reprisal, you can also complain directly to the Commission.
points: Police and mandatory reporting where a child is involved

title: Biohazard Management
description: Give workers the knowledge to handle blood, body fluids, sharps and contaminated items safely in home and community settings.
standards: Safe Environment; Management of Waste; WHS duties

steps.title: What counts as a biohazard
paragraphs: A biohazard is something that can carry infection. In support work that means blood, urine, faeces, vomit, saliva, and fluid from a wound. You treat them as infectious even when the person is well and even when you know them. You do not decide by looking that a fluid is 'only a little bit' and therefore safe.

Sharps are needles, lancets, razors, and anything else that can puncture skin. Contaminated dressings, continence aids, and used gloves or gowns are biohazards too, because fluid sits on them. They do not go loose in a kitchen bin, a handbag, or the back of a car. You contain them, and you clean your hands after.
points: Blood, urine, faeces, vomit, saliva and wound fluids
Contaminated dressings, continence aids and PPE

steps.title: Standard precautions
paragraphs: Standard precautions are the habits you use with every person, on every shift, whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Treat every body fluid as infectious. That protects the participant and you, and it avoids treating one person as 'the infectious one'.

Choose protective equipment for the task in front of you. Gloves for personal care and body fluids. An apron or gown if fluid may splash your clothes. Eye and mask protection if fluid may hit your face. Clean your hands before you touch the person and again after you remove gloves. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. They come off between tasks, and your hands are cleaned again.
points: Treat all body fluids as infectious

steps.title: Spills and clean-up
paragraphs: A spill kit holds what you need before you start: gloves, an apron, eye protection if there is splash, absorbent material, a disinfectant the provider uses, bags, and a scoop or scraper. Know where it is in the house or the vehicle before you need it. Do not go looking for a tea towel once blood is on the floor.

The order is contain, absorb, clean, disinfect, dispose. Stop the spill spreading, soak it up, clean the surface, then disinfect for the contact time on the product. Clothing and linen that are soiled go into a bag at the point of use, not shaken out in the hallway. Wash them as the provider directs, separately from ordinary washing when that is the instruction. Then clean your hands.

steps.title: Sharps and waste
paragraphs: Used sharps go straight into an approved sharps container, at the place you used them. The container is rigid, labelled, and not filled past the line. It is not a drink bottle, a plastic bag, or the kitchen bin.

Never recap a needle, and never bend or snap it. Most needle-stick injuries happen when someone tries to make a used needle 'safer' by hand. Clinical waste (material soaked with blood or body fluid) is a different stream from ordinary household rubbish. If you are unsure which bag to use, ask before you throw it in with the recycling or the kitchen waste.

steps.title: If you are exposed
paragraphs: If a needle punctures your skin, let the wound bleed, wash it with soap and water, and do not scrub or suck it. If fluid splashes your eyes, mouth, or broken skin, rinse with plenty of water. Do this immediately, before you finish the rest of the task.

Tell your supervisor the same shift and get medical advice straight away. Some exposures need treatment within hours, so waiting until tomorrow is the wrong call. Write down what happened, what fluid it was, and what you did. That record is how you get the right follow-up, and how the next person avoids the same exposure.

title: Bullying Prevention for Support Workers
description: Help workers recognise bullying, know the difference from reasonable management action, and use the provider's process to raise it.
standards: NDIS Code of Conduct; WHS psychosocial hazards; Fair Work anti-bullying provisions

steps.title: What bullying is and is not
paragraphs: Bullying at work is repeated unreasonable behaviour that creates a risk to health and safety. It is not a single sharp comment, and it is not a personality clash on its own. It becomes bullying when it is repeated and a reasonable person would see a risk to someone's health.

It can look like being left out of handovers, intimidated on a shift, loaded with the tasks no one else will do, or humiliated in front of a participant. Reasonable management action is different. A supervisor can raise performance, change a roster fairly, or give a lawful direction, if they do it reasonably. A single incident can still be harassment or assault and still needs a response. It is just not called bullying unless it is repeated.
points: Repeated unreasonable behaviour creating a risk to health and safety

steps.title: Bullying in support settings
paragraphs: Shared shifts make bullying easy to hide. It can be two workers freezing a third out of decisions, mocking how they support someone, or dumping the heavy personal care on them every time. The participant feels that atmosphere even when the words are not aimed at them.

Workers can also bully participants: controlling their day, mocking their speech or body, withholding a drink, a cigarette, or a community outing as punishment. Group chats and roster apps count. Messages that humiliate a colleague or a participant are still bullying when they are repeated. Screenshot them and report them. Do not pile on, and do not forward them for a joke.

steps.title: Impact
paragraphs: Bullying causes psychosocial injury. People lose sleep, dread shifts, make mistakes, and eventually leave. That injury is real even when there is no bruise.

The support gets worse. A frightened worker rushes personal care, skips a handover, or stops speaking up when something is unsafe. A participant who is mocked stops asking for help. If you see it and say nothing, you are part of how it continues. You do not have to confront the person in the moment if that is unsafe. You do have to tell someone who can act.

steps.title: What to do
paragraphs: Speak up early if you can do it safely. A calm sentence — 'that handover left me out, and I need to be included' — sometimes stops a pattern before it sets. If it continues, or if you are not safe to say it, use the reporting pathway. You can tell your team leader, and you can go around them if they are the person involved. The report is kept as confidential as the investigation allows.

Use the employee assistance program or another support if the behaviour is affecting your health. You do not have to wait until you are in crisis. In more serious cases a worker can apply to the Fair Work Commission for an order to stop bullying. That sits alongside the provider's process. It does not replace telling the provider what is happening.

title: Leading and Communicating Change
description: Prepare team leaders to introduce changes (new rosters, policies, systems, Practice Standards revisions) in a way that keeps workers engaged and participants' supports stable.
standards: Governance and Operational Management; Quality Management; Continuity of Supports

steps.title: Why change is hard in support work
paragraphs: Support teams are often casual, split across houses, and working while the people they support are asleep or out. A change announced in one meeting misses most of the workforce. People hear a fragment on a shift and fill the gaps with rumour.

Teams also carry change fatigue. A new roster, a new app, and a new form in the same month feel like the work is never allowed to settle. Trust depends on what happened last time. If the last change was sprung on people, or a promise was broken, they will hear the next message as a threat. You plan for that. You do not call them resistant for remembering.

steps.title: Planning the message
paragraphs: Say what is changing, why, when it starts, and what is staying the same. People cope better when they can see the edge of the change. 'Everything is different from Monday' is not a message they can use on a shift.

Tell leaders first, so they can answer questions instead of learning the news from their team. Then tell workers, then tell participants and families in plain language if the change touches their support. Pick channels that reach a dispersed workforce: a short written note they can read on a phone, plus a conversation on shift. A single email to a shared inbox is not a plan.

steps.title: Handling resistance
paragraphs: Listen before you persuade. A worker who says a new manual-handling plan will not work at 6am in that bathroom may be right. Ask what they are worried about, and separate a practical concern from a refusal to change at all.

When the concern is valid, change the plan. Forcing a procedure that cannot be done safely teaches people to ignore the next one. When the concern is preference rather than safety or the participant's rights, explain the reason again and hold the change. You can acknowledge that it is inconvenient and still ask them to do it.

title: Maintaining Professional Boundaries
description: Help workers hold the line between a warm, respectful relationship and one that becomes personal, financial, romantic or dependent, in settings where the work happens in someone's home.
standards: NDIS Code of Conduct; Rights and Responsibilities: Privacy and Dignity; Independence and Informed Choice

steps.title: Why boundaries matter
paragraphs: You are in someone's home, often helping with the most private parts of their life. Warmth is part of good support. A personal, financial, or romantic relationship is not. The power sits with you: you are paid, you can leave, and you know the system. They may depend on you for care they cannot get from anyone else that day.

A dual relationship is when you are also their friend, their lender, their tenant, or their partner. Dependence makes it hard for them to say no to you. What feels like closeness to you can be exploitation to them, even if they seem to agree. Boundaries protect the relationship so the support can stay safe.

steps.title: Where boundaries drift
paragraphs: Drift usually starts small. A gift, a loan of twenty dollars, a lift that is not on the roster, a social media follow. Then contact outside work, private arrangements the provider does not know about, and telling the person your own problems so they end up caring for you.

Physical affection and romantic or sexual interest are a hard line. A participant may want closeness. Your job is to keep the relationship as support. You do not start a relationship with someone you support, and you do not continue one. Gifts of significant value, lending money either way, and using their card are financial boundaries. If you are unsure whether something is a drift, it is already time to tell your supervisor.

steps.title: Under the Code of Conduct
paragraphs: The NDIS Code of Conduct requires you to act with integrity. That means the support is for the participant, the records are true, and your private interests do not steer their choices.

Sexual misconduct toward a participant is always a reportable incident. There is no version of it that stays between you. Conflicts of interest are disclosed. If your family member works for a provider you might recommend, or you would benefit from a decision, you say so before the decision is made. Hiding it is the breach, even if the decision would have been the same.

title: NDIS Induction
description: The onboarding pathway for every new worker. Covers how the NDIS works, rights-based practice, safeguarding, WHS, positive behaviour support and inclusive communication. Reinforces but does not replace the Commission's Worker Orientation Module.
standards: Human Resource Management (induction before delivering supports); all four Core Module outcomes at introductory level

steps.title: Module 1: How the NDIS works
paragraphs: The NDIA funds the scheme and approves plans. The NDIS Commission regulates providers and workers and handles complaints and reportable incidents. Providers, registered or not, deliver the supports. You work for a provider. You are not the NDIA, and you do not change someone's plan on the day.

A plan sets the person's goals and a budget, split into support categories. You deliver what is funded and agreed, and you do not invent extra hours to fill a budget. The Practice Standards describe the support a person should receive: safe, competent, and directed by them. Registered providers work to those standards. Unregistered providers still follow the Code of Conduct.
points: The Practice Standards and why they matter to you

steps.title: Module 2: Rights and person-centred practice
paragraphs: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the NDIS Act start from the same place: people with disability have the same rights as everyone else. Your shift is one of the places those rights are either real or ignored.

Choice and control means the person decides what happens in their day, as far as they can, with support to understand the options. Dignity of risk means they may choose something you would not choose, and you do not take the choice away unless there is a serious risk of harm you cannot reduce another way. Privacy and consent mean you ask before you touch, before you share information, and before you invite someone else into the room.

steps.title: Module 3: Safeguarding
paragraphs: Abuse and neglect have types you should be able to name: physical, sexual, emotional, financial, and neglect. You act on signs, you do not wait for proof, and you report through the provider the same shift. Restrictive practices — seclusion, chemical, mechanical, physical, and environmental restraint — are not ordinary tools. They are used only as a behaviour support plan allows.

An incident is something that harmed someone or could have. Some incidents are reportable to the Commission, usually within 24 hours. You record the facts and tell your supervisor. A participant can complain about their support, including about you. You help them do it. You do not talk them out of it, and you do not retaliate.

steps.title: Module 4: Working safely
paragraphs: Work health and safety applies in someone's lounge room as much as in an office. You look for hazards, you follow the safe way to move and transfer, and you stop if a task will injure you or them. Infection control is part of every shift: clean hands, cover coughs, use protective equipment for the task, and handle waste safely.

Medication is done only in the way you are authorised and trained. You do not guess a dose or borrow someone else's supply. Progress notes say what support happened, how the person responded, and anything the next worker must know. If it is not written, the next person is supporting them blind.

steps.title: Module 5: Supporting behaviour
paragraphs: Behaviour communicates a need: pain, fear, boredom, sensory overload, a wish to stop, or a wish for company. You look for the need before you look for a consequence. Positive behaviour support builds a life the person wants, and uses proactive strategies so restraint is needed less. The practitioner writes the plan. You implement it as written.

Trauma-informed support means you expect that past harm may shape how someone reacts to touch, bathrooms, raised voices, or being told what to do. You offer predictability and choice. De-escalation is your voice, your distance, and a smaller demand. You also keep yourself safe. Leaving a room to get help is a valid response. You do not trade your safety, or theirs, to finish a task.

steps.title: Module 6: Communication and conduct
paragraphs: Inclusive communication means the person gets information in a way they can use: speech, pictures, a device, Easy Read, or time to process. You wait. You do not finish their sentences and call it support. Cultural safety means you ask what matters to them — culture, faith, family, identity — and you change the support to fit, rather than asking them to fit the roster.

The Code of Conduct has seven obligations. In short: respect rights, respect privacy, work safely and within your competence, be honest, raise concerns, and prevent violence, abuse, neglect, and exploitation. You stay inside your role. Warmth is part of the work. A personal, financial, or sexual relationship is not.

title: Person-Centred Active Support
description: Teach the practical skill of doing with, not for: supporting people to take part in every activity of daily life at whatever level they can, rather than having things done to them.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Person-centred supports; Independence and informed choice; Provision of Supports: Responsive support provision

steps.title: Why active support
paragraphs: Active support means the person takes part in their own life, at whatever level they can, instead of having life done to them. Engagement — doing, choosing, being with people — is what makes a day feel like theirs. Quality of life is that participation, not a tidy house.

The hotel model is the opposite. Workers cook, clean, and decide, and the person waits. It looks efficient and it shrinks someone's skills. Research on active support shows that when staff step back to the right amount of help, people do more and spend less time disengaged. Your job is to enable, not to complete the task fastest.

steps.title: The four essentials
paragraphs: Every moment has potential. Folding one towel, choosing a shirt, or stirring a pot counts. You do not wait for a program called 'activities'. Little and often beats a long session nobody can sustain. Graded assistance is the skill: ask, then instruct, then prompt, then show, then guide physically. You start with the least help that works, and you add help only for the step they cannot do yet.
Choice and control run through all of it. You offer real options, not a pretend choice after you have already decided. If they pick the option that takes longer, that is the support working.
points: Graded assistance: ask, instruct, prompt, show, guide

steps.title: Task analysis
paragraphs: Break the task into steps small enough to see which one the person can do. Making tea might be: get the cup, put the bag in, pour the water, carry it. They may do three of those and need you for the kettle. The support is the one step, not the whole job taken over.

Change the environment so the step is possible. A cup on the bench instead of in a high cupboard. A chair at the bench. Ingredients out. You are looking for the step they can own, then handing that step to them every time, so it stays theirs.

steps.title: In practice
paragraphs: Use this in ordinary tasks: preparing a meal, putting on a wash, unpacking shopping, paying for a coffee. Talk through the next step and then wait. Match their pace. Filling the silence by doing it yourself is how active support disappears.

If the person declines, that is a choice. You can offer again later or offer a smaller part. You do not take the task over as a punishment, and you do not insist in order to tick a goal. Record that they declined and what you offered, so the team does not read the day as 'did not engage'.

title: Slips, Trips and Falls
description: Reduce the most common injury to both workers and participants in homes, group settings and offices.
standards: Safe Environment; WHS duties; Risk Management

steps.title: Hazards
paragraphs: Most slips and trips are ordinary: a wet bathroom floor, a loose rug, a cord across a walkway, clutter, a dim hallway, shoes with no grip. You notice them at the start of the shift, before you walk someone through them.

Steps, kerbs, and getting in and out of a vehicle are where falls happen outside. In an office, the hazards are cables, boxes in walkways, and stairs with something in your hands. You move the hazard or you change the route. You do not step over it all shift and hope.
points: Wet floors, loose rugs, cords, clutter, poor lighting, footwear

steps.title: Participant falls risk
paragraphs: Falls risk rises with some medicines, poor vision, the wrong or missing mobility aid, rushing to the toilet, and changes in thinking or alertness. A person who has fallen before is more likely to fall again. Read that history before you work out how to support them to move.

A falls risk assessment sets the plan: which aid, which route, whether someone stays beside them, what footwear. You follow it. If today they are dizzy, more tired, or without their usual glasses, you reassess in the moment and slow down. You do not stick to yesterday's plan when today is different.

steps.title: After a fall
paragraphs: Do not lift a person who has fallen. Lifting injures your back and can worsen their injury. Look at them, talk to them, and call for help as the plan and the situation require. If they hit their head, or they take blood-thinning medicine, treat that as urgent and get medical advice even if they say they are fine.

Then report the incident, including a near miss if they almost fell. Say where, what they were doing, and what the environment was like. That is how the next fall is prevented, not how blame is assigned.
points: Do not lift; assess; call for help

title: Supported Decision-Making
description: Show workers how to support a person to make their own decisions rather than making decisions for them, including people with cognitive disability and people under guardianship.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Independence and informed choice; Individual values and beliefs; NDIS Act principles

steps.title: Rights and capacity
paragraphs: Every adult is presumed able to make their own decisions. Disability, a guardian, or a hard decision does not cancel that presumption. You start by supporting the decision, not by taking it.

Capacity is decision-specific. A person may decide what to eat and need support to decide about a medical procedure. You do not treat 'has a cognitive disability' as 'cannot decide anything'. The standard you are aiming at is their will and preferences — what they want — not what you believe is in their best interests. Best interests is the old habit of deciding for people.
points: Will and preferences versus best interests

steps.title: Supported versus substitute
paragraphs: Supported decision-making is a range. You explain, you wait, you offer options, you involve a person they trust. Substitute decision-making is someone else deciding in their place. A guardian, an administrator, or a nominee has authority only for the decisions in their order. Read what it actually covers.

A guardian for accommodation does not automatically decide dinner, clothes, or who visits. An administrator manages money, not relationships. If you are unsure, ask to see the order rather than handing the decision to a family member who sounds confident. When the person can decide, they decide, even if a guardian exists for other matters.
points: What a guardian can and cannot decide

steps.title: Strategies

steps.title: Dignity of risk
paragraphs: People are allowed to make choices you disagree with: the less healthy meal, the relationship you worry about, the outing that will be tiring. You explain the risk in a way they can understand. You do not take the choice away because you would choose differently.

Duty of care still applies when serious harm is likely and cannot be reduced another way. That is a high bar, not a reason to run someone's life. When you have a risk-enablement conversation, write what they understood, what they decided, and what you will do to make the choice safer. The note shows the decision was theirs.

title: Supporting Human Rights
description: Ground every worker in the rights framework the NDIS is built on, and show what those rights look like in an ordinary shift.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: all outcomes; UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; NDIS Act 2013 objects and principles

steps.title: Models of disability
paragraphs: The medical model locates the problem in the person's body or mind and tries to fix them. The charity model sees them as someone to be pitied and helped. The social model says people are disabled by barriers: stairs, attitudes, inflexible routines. The human rights model says they are rights-holders, and support exists so they can live on equal terms.

Language follows the model. 'Suffering from', 'wheelchair-bound', and 'non-compliant' put the problem in the person. Talk about the person first, the support they use, and the barrier in front of them. Attitudes show up in small acts: talking to the worker instead of the person, deciding they will not want to come, calling a choice 'behaviour'.
points: Medical, charity, social and human rights models

steps.title: The rights framework
paragraphs: The UN Convention sets out rights that matter on a shift: equality, accessibility, living independently, privacy, health, and being free from exploitation and abuse. You will not quote article numbers at the door. You will notice when a routine cancels one of those rights.

The NDIS Act principles say people have the same rights as other Australians, and they should be able to exercise choice. The Disability Discrimination Act makes it unlawful to treat someone less favourably because of disability. A provider's convenience is not a defence.

steps.title: Rights in daily practice
paragraphs: On an ordinary shift, rights look like privacy during personal care, dignity in how you speak, choice about food and clothes and visitors, taking part in household life, relationships the person wants, and sexuality that is not treated as a problem. These are not extras after the tasks. They are the support.

Organisational routines override rights when everyone showers at 7 because the roster says so, or when bedrooms are locked 'for safety' without an authorisation. A restrictive practice is a rights issue first. It removes freedom. It is allowed only as a last resort, in a plan, and it should be reducing.

steps.title: When rights and rules collide
paragraphs: Dignity of risk is the collision you will meet most often. The person wants to do something that carries a risk. You inform them, you reduce what you can, and you respect the choice unless serious harm cannot be prevented any other way.

If a practice limits rights — a blanket rule, a locked cupboard, a decision made by staff for convenience — raise it. Tell your supervisor what you saw and whose right it affects. Advocacy services exist so the person does not have to argue alone. Help them contact one if they want that. Do not talk them out of it.

title: Trauma Informed Support
description: Help workers understand how trauma shapes behaviour and relationships, and support in ways that do not re-traumatise.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Person-centred supports; Provision of Supports: Responsive support provision

steps.title: Understanding trauma
paragraphs: Trauma is the lasting effect of an event or a life that overwhelmed a person's ability to cope. A single incident is one event. Complex trauma is repeated harm, often in relationships. Developmental trauma happens in childhood, while the brain and the sense of safety are still forming. Many people with disability have lived with one or more of these, including in institutions and out-of-home care.

Trauma changes the brain and body. Alarm systems stay on. Touch, a closed door, a raised voice, or a loss of control can feel like the original harm, even when this shift is kind. You are not treating trauma. You are supporting in a way that does not set that alarm off.
points: Prevalence in disability, out-of-home care and institutions
Effect on the brain and body

steps.title: Recognising responses
paragraphs: Fight, flight, freeze, and fawn are survival responses, not attitudes. Fight can look like shouting or hitting. Flight can look like leaving or refusing to enter a room. Freeze can look like silence and stillness that gets called 'non-compliance'. Fawn can look like agreeing to everything, including things they do not want, because agreement used to keep them safe.

Common triggers in care are touch, bathrooms, being naked, raised voices, being rushed, and being told what to do with no choice. The behaviour is communication. Ask what just happened, reduce the demand, and follow the plan. Do not punish a survival response.
points: Triggers in care settings: touch, bathrooms, raised voices, being told what to do

steps.title: Principles in practice
paragraphs: Predictability and choice lower the alarm. Say what will happen next, and offer a real choice about order, clothing, or who is in the room. Ask before you touch, every time, including people you have supported for years. Consent is not a one-off signature.

Build routines with the person, not for them. A routine they helped design is safer than one imposed 'because it works'. Cultural safety matters here too. What feels respectful in one community can feel exposing in another. Ask, and follow what they and their people tell you.

steps.title: Avoiding re-traumatisation
paragraphs: Restrictive practices replay the experience of being overpowered. Use them only as an authorised last resort, and treat every use as a serious event, not a technique. Language of power and control — 'you have to', 'because I said', 'don't make me' — tells the body it is not safe.

After a difficult moment, repair. Come back calm, say what happened in simple words, and restore choice. Do not pretend it did not happen, and do not lecture. A short, respectful return teaches that the relationship survived.

steps.title: Worker wellbeing
paragraphs: Vicarious trauma is the effect on you of hearing and seeing other people's harm, over and over. It can make you numb, cynical, or constantly on edge. That changes the support. A numb worker misses signs. An on-edge worker escalates situations.

Use supervision and debrief to put the shift down, not to gossip about the person. Keep boundaries so their trauma does not become your private relationship with them. If you are not sleeping, or you dread a particular shift, tell your team leader before it becomes the way you work.

title: NDIS Code of Conduct
description: Make sure every worker, in every role, knows the seven obligations of the Code, how the Commission enforces them, and what each one looks like in practice.
standards: NDIS (Code of Conduct) Rules 2018; mapped to all four Core Modules

steps.title: Who the Code covers
paragraphs: The NDIS Code of Conduct applies to registered and unregistered providers, and to every worker: support workers, team leaders, contractors, and office staff. Registration is not the thing that creates the duty.

Office staff are covered because they handle money, rosters, records, and complaints. A rostering decision or a privacy breach in the office can harm a participant as surely as a bad shift. If your work touches a participant's life, the Code applies to you.
points: All workers, including office and contractors

steps.title: The seven elements
paragraphs: Act with respect for individual rights, including choice and dignity of risk. Respect privacy. Provide supports safely and competently, which means you do not do tasks you are not trained and authorised to do. Act with integrity, honesty, and transparency, including about conflicts of interest.

Promptly raise and act on concerns about quality and safety. Do not wait to see if someone else notices. Take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to violence, exploitation, neglect, and abuse. 'I didn't want to dob' is not one of the elements. There is a seventh obligation in the Code's guidance about not engaging in sexual misconduct. Sexual contact with a participant is never part of the job.
points: Act with respect for individual rights

Promptly raise and act on quality and safety concerns
Take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse

steps.title: Elements in practice
paragraphs: Each obligation shows up differently by role. A support worker respects rights by offering a real choice at breakfast. An admin worker respects rights by not deciding a service is 'too hard' without talking to the person. A leader respects rights by refusing a house rule that locks everyone's food away.

Privacy is a closed bathroom door, and it is also not leaving a participant's plan open on a reception desk. Competence is refusing a hoist you have not been shown. Integrity is writing the note for the shift you actually worked. Raising a concern is telling someone the same day that a participant flinched when a colleague came in. Preventing abuse is interrupting mockery, not laughing along.
points: One scenario per element across support, admin and leadership roles

title: Privacy, Dignity and Information Handling
description: How to protect a participant's personal and health information, share it only with consent and on a need-to-know basis, and keep their dignity during personal care and in records.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Privacy and Dignity; Governance: Information Management; Privacy Act 1988 Australian Privacy Principles; Notifiable Data Breaches scheme

steps.title: What information is protected
paragraphs: Personal information identifies someone: name, address, photo, date of birth. Sensitive information includes health, disability, and sexuality. Health information is the plans, diagnoses, medication, and notes you write. All of it is protected. Curiosity is not a reason to open a file.

The Australian Privacy Principles, in plain terms, mean you collect only what you need, you use it for the reason it was given, you keep it accurate, you store it safely, and the person can ask to see it. Participant records, photos, plans, and progress notes are all in scope. A photo on your phone is a record, not a souvenir.

steps.title: Consent and sharing
paragraphs: Informed consent means the person understands what will be shared, with whom, and why, and they agree. If a guardian has authority for that decision, the guardian can consent within the order. A family member who is not the guardian does not automatically get the file.

Sharing with family, another provider, or the NDIA needs a reason and consent, unless a law requires the disclosure, such as a serious safety report. Inside your organisation, need-to-know means the next worker on the shift hears what they need to support the person. The whole group chat does not.

steps.title: Privacy and dignity in practice
paragraphs: During personal care, shut the door, close the curtain, cover the person, and ask before you start. Talk to them, not about them, while you work. Other people in the house do not get a commentary.

Do not discuss a participant in a cafe, in a shop queue, or in the car where other passengers can hear the details. Photos and social media are out unless there is specific consent for that photo and that use. A face in the background of your story is still their face.

steps.title: Data breaches
paragraphs: A breach is when personal information is lost, accessed, or sent where it should not be. A stolen laptop, a photo in the wrong chat, a bag left on the bus, an email to the wrong family. If you are not sure, treat it as a breach.

Contain it immediately. Recall the message if you can, lock the device, tell the people who received it not to forward it. Then report internally straight away so the provider can judge whether it is a notifiable breach. Do not wait to see if anyone complains, and do not delete the evidence to make the problem smaller.

title: Cultural Safety and Working with Diversity
description: How to support Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people from culturally and linguistically diverse communities, people of faith, and LGBTIQA+ participants so the support feels safe to them.
standards: Rights and Responsibilities: Individual values and beliefs; Person-centred supports; NDIS Act principles

steps.title: Cultural safety
paragraphs: Cultural awareness is knowing differences exist. Sensitivity is not offending on purpose. Competence is having some skills. Safety is decided by the person receiving the support, not by you. If they do not feel safe to be themselves with you, the support is not culturally safe, however polite you were.

Unconscious bias is the assumption you do not notice: who you explain things to, whose family you trust, whose pain you take seriously. Slow down when you notice you have decided what someone will want before you asked.
points: Who decides whether care is safe

steps.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander participants
paragraphs: History matters. Removal, institutions, and racism in health and disability systems are why trust is not automatic. You earn it by listening, by not rushing, and by not requiring someone to tell their story to get basic respect.

Family, community, and Country shape decisions. The right person to involve may not be the person on the intake form. Work with Aboriginal Community Controlled organisations when the person wants that. Do not position yourself as the expert on their culture.

title: Building Resilience to Stress in Support Work
description: Reduce burnout and turnover by giving workers practical tools to manage the emotional load of support work.
standards: Human Resource Management (worker support and supervision); WHS psychosocial hazards

steps.title: Stress in support work
paragraphs: Support work carries a particular load. You are in someone's home, you deal with pain, distress, and families, and you often work alone. Common stressors are unpredictable behaviour, time pressure, grief when someone declines, and conflict about how a shift should go. Acute stress is the spike during a hard hour. Chronic stress is what is still in your body on your day off.

Compassion fatigue is when caring goes numb. Vicarious trauma is when other people's harm starts to live in you. Both make you less able to notice risk and more likely to snap or withdraw. Naming them is the start of doing something about them. They are not a personal weakness, and they are not something you hide until you resign.

steps.title: Warning signs
paragraphs: Watch your body and your mood. Headaches, poor sleep, a short fuse, dreading a particular house, and drinking more to come down after a shift are signs. Cynicism and detachment show up as jokes at a participant's expense, or as doing the minimum and calling it 'being professional'. Mistakes follow: a missed medication check, a rough transfer, a note you do not write.

Those signs are a safety issue, not only a wellbeing issue. The quality of the support drops before you admit you are not coping. If you notice them in yourself, tell your team leader. If you notice them in a colleague, say something to them or to a leader. Leaving it as gossip does not help them or the people they support.
points: The link to quality and safety of supports

paragraphs: Before a shift, read the plan and decide what you will not take on that is outside your role. Boundaries are a stress strategy. Know the tasks, the risks, and who you will call. During the shift, slow one thing down. A breath before you respond, a glass of water, finishing one task before you start the next. Pacing is how you stay kind at the end of the shift, not only at the start.

After the shift, debrief what actually happened, then leave it. Change your clothes, eat, do something that is not the job. If the same house sits in your chest every time, that is information for supervision, not a secret you push through.

title: Bullying Awareness for Disability Support Leaders
description: Give team leaders and managers the skills to prevent bullying, respond to reports properly, and avoid becoming the source of it.
standards: Human Resource Management; WHS psychosocial hazards; positive duty

steps.title: Leader duties
paragraphs: Leaders have a work health and safety duty to manage psychosocial risk. Bullying, harassment, and unreasonable job demands are hazards, the same as a broken hoist. You identify them, you control them, and you do not wait for a formal complaint before you act.

There is also a positive duty to prevent sexual harassment, not only to respond after it. Vicarious liability means the organisation can be responsible for what a leader ignored. If you know a pattern is happening on your shifts and you leave it, that is your decision, and it has consequences for the people in that team.
points: WHS duty to manage psychosocial risk

steps.title: Reasonable management action
paragraphs: You can manage performance. You can change a roster, correct a technique, and require a note to be rewritten. That is reasonable management action when the reason is real, the process is fair, and the tone does not humiliate. Doing it in front of a participant, or by text at midnight, is how management becomes bullying.

Common mistakes are storing up grievances and delivering them as a character attack, applying a rule to one worker that others ignore, and calling punishment 'feedback'. Write down the behaviour you saw, the effect, and what needs to change. Give the person a chance to respond. Document the conversation.

steps.title: Responding to a report
paragraphs: The first conversation is to understand and to make the person safe enough to keep working. Listen. Do not explain the other person's intentions. Do not ask them to sort it out themselves if the behaviour is serious or the power is uneven.

Put interim measures in place: separate rosters, a different supervisor, a check-in. Tell them what support exists. Decide whether this needs an investigation and who should run it. You do not investigate your own close friend. Keep a record of what you were told, what you did, and when. A report that lives only in your memory is not a response.

title: Coaching Conversations: A Course for Team Leaders
description: Turn supervision from a compliance tick into a conversation that improves practice, using a simple coaching structure.
standards: Human Resource Management (supervision, support and performance)

steps.title: What supervision is for
paragraphs: Supervision is where a worker gets support, gets better at the work, and is held to the standard the participant needs. It is a conversation about practice. A tick on a form, with nothing discussed, is not supervision.

Write down what you talked about and what you agreed, so the next conversation can start there. The note exists so the worker's skill grows and so anyone looking later can see the support was real. If the note could describe any worker on any day, it was not a conversation.

steps.title: A coaching structure
paragraphs: A simple structure keeps the conversation useful. Goal: what are we trying to improve for the person they support. Reality: what is actually happening on shift. Options: what they could do differently. Way forward: what they will try before you meet again, and what you will do to help.

Ask open questions and then wait. 'What happened when you offered the choice?' teaches more than 'Next time, do it this way.' The urge to solve is strong, and it steals the learning. Give advice when there is a safety rule they must follow. Otherwise, help them find the next step.

description: Core communication skills for the whole workforce: listening, clear speaking, handover, and accessible communication with participants.

steps.title: Listening
paragraphs: Active listening is attention you can see. Put the phone down, face the person, and let them finish. In support work you are often planning the next task while they are still talking. They can tell.

Reflect and summarise. 'You want the shower after breakfast, not before.' That checks you heard them, and it slows you down. Barriers are noise, time pressure, assuming you already know, and listening only for the moment you can speak. Name the barrier when it is yours.

steps.title: Speaking clearly
paragraphs: Plain language is short words and one idea at a time. 'I will help you with your jumper' beats a sentence full of service jargon. Handover tells the next worker what they need: how the person is, what happened, what is unfinished, and any risk. It is not a story about your shift.

Assertive means you say the thing that keeps someone safe, without attacking. 'I am not going to lift without the hoist' is assertive. Shouting it, or sulking and doing the lift anyway, is not. You can be warm and still be clear.

paragraphs: Use the communication plan. Some people use a device, pictures, signs, or behaviour. Easy Read and visuals are tools, not decorations. Offer them when the decision matters.

title: Fire Safety Essentials
description: Every worker knows how fire starts, how to prevent it, and what to do when the alarm goes, in an office, a group home or a participant's own home.
standards: Emergency and Disaster Management; Safe Environment; WHS duties; state fire safety regulations

steps.title: Prevention
paragraphs: Fires in support settings start in ordinary ways: cooking left on, a heater near a curtain, smoking, oxygen used near a flame, a device charging on a bed. Oxygen and smoking or candles do not go together. Say so every time, including to visitors.

Keep exits clear. A hoist, a pile of donations, or a locked screen door can trap someone who cannot move quickly. Test smoke alarms the way the house plan says. If one is chirping or missing, report it the same day. Do not take the battery out to stop the noise and leave it.
points: Cooking, heaters, smoking, oxygen, charging devices

steps.title: When fire starts
paragraphs: RACE is the order: remove people from immediate danger, alert others and call 000, contain the fire by closing a door if you can do it on the way out, and extinguish only if it is small and you know how. Evacuation beats heroics.

Call 000 early. Give the address, say who cannot walk out unaided, and say if oxygen or other hazards are inside. Never go back in for belongings, pets, or a phone. Tell firefighters who is unaccounted for and where their room is.
points: RACE: remove, alert, contain, extinguish or evacuate

steps.title: Evacuating participants
paragraphs: A personal emergency evacuation plan says how this person gets out, who helps, what equipment comes, and where you meet. Read it before you need it. A plan in a folder you have never opened will fail at 2am.

Wheelchairs, hoists, and stairs need a method decided in advance. You do not invent a carry during the fire. Sensory and cognitive needs matter: a loud alarm may make someone freeze or run the wrong way. If they refuse to leave, use the plan's approach, keep your voice calm, and do not leave them inside alone while you save yourself without telling firefighters exactly where they are.
points: Sensory and cognitive needs; refusal to leave

steps.title: Extinguishers and blankets
paragraphs: Extinguisher types match the fire. Water on a cooking-oil fire or an electrical fire makes it worse. Know which extinguisher is in the house and what it is for. A fire blanket smothers a small pan fire. Turn the heat off if you can do it safely.

PASS is pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep. If the fire is bigger than a waste bin, if smoke is thick, or if you do not know what is burning, do not fight it. Get people out and close the door.
points: Types and what they are for

title: Handling Complaints and Difficult Conversations
description: Every worker must know the provider's complaints system and how to help a participant use it. This course covers receiving a complaint, responding without defensiveness, and what happens next.
standards: Feedback and Complaints Management; NDIS (Complaints Management and Resolution) Rules 2018
requirement_status: Explicitly required (workers must be trained in the complaints system)

steps.title: The right to complain
paragraphs: Every participant has the right to complain about their support, including about you, and to have that complaint taken seriously. The rules and the Practice Standards require a system that is easy to use and free of reprisal. A complaint is also information. It tells you where the support is failing while you can still fix it.

No one is punished for complaining. Shifts are not quietly cut, and workers do not become cold. An advocate can help the person complain. You offer that. You do not decide they are 'not the complaining type'.

steps.title: Receiving a complaint
paragraphs: Any worker can receive a complaint. You do not tell someone to put it in writing before you will listen, and you do not send them away because you are 'not the manager'. Listen, thank them, and write down who, what happened, when, and what they want to happen.

Hand it on within the time your process sets, usually quickly. A complaint that stays in your notebook is a complaint you buried. Tell the person what will happen next and when they will hear back. Then do not argue the facts in the doorway.
points: What to record: who, what, when, desired outcome
Handing it on within the timeframe

steps.title: Difficult conversations
paragraphs: Stay calm when someone is angry. Acknowledge the feeling before you talk about the process. 'You are furious that the shift did not happen. I want to get this down properly.' Defend the organisation later, if at all, not in the first five minutes.

Do not admit legal fault you do not have authority to admit, and do not deny something you have not looked at. Close with the next step: who will contact them, and when. A conversation that ends with 'we'll see' teaches people that complaining is pointless.
points: Not defending, not admitting fault prematurely

steps.title: The process
paragraphs: Acknowledge the complaint in the timeframe, in a way the person understands. Then assess it. Some complaints need a conversation and a change. Some need a proper investigation because someone may have been harmed. Do not downgrade a safety issue into 'feedback' to keep the numbers tidy.

Resolution means the person hears the outcome, including when you disagree, and what will change. Then look at whether the same issue is sitting in other houses. One complaint about missed showers is a reason to check the roster, not a file you close and forget.

title: Handling Incidents
description: Every worker must know what an incident is, what to do when one happens, and which incidents the Commission must be told about and when.
standards: Incident Management; NDIS (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018
requirement_status: Explicitly required (workers must be trained in the incident management system)

steps.title: What is an incident
paragraphs: An incident is an act, an omission, an event, or a circumstance that harmed a participant or a worker, or could have. Dropping someone, missing a medication, a participant hurting someone, abuse, a fall, a missing person. Near misses count. The hoist sling that nearly failed is how you prevent the next one. If you only record injuries, you only learn after someone is hurt.

Incidents include a participant harming another person, a worker, or themselves. You still record it. You do not call it 'just behaviour' and leave it out of the incident system. The behaviour plan and the incident record do different jobs.
points: Acts, omissions, events and circumstances that cause harm or could have
Near misses and why they matter
Incidents involving the participant harming others

steps.title: Responding
paragraphs: Make people safe and get medical help first. First aid, an ambulance, separating people, turning off a hazard. Comfort the person in a way they can use. Do not interview them for the perfect note while they are injured or terrified.

Notify the person your process names, as soon as the immediate danger is under control. Serious harm is a phone call, not a message at the end of the shift. Stay with the situation until someone has taken it over or you are told you can leave.

steps.title: Recording
paragraphs: Write facts. What you saw, what you heard, what you did, and the time. 'He was aggressive' is an opinion. 'He hit the table with his fist and said he wanted to leave' is a fact. Leave out diagnoses and guesses about motive.
Write it the same day, in the incident system, not only in a progress note. The register is how patterns are seen. A fall every Tuesday that lives in six different notebooks is invisible.

steps.title: Reportable incidents
paragraphs: Some incidents must be notified to the NDIS Commission. Death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact, and sexual misconduct are notified within 24 hours. Unauthorised use of a restrictive practice is notified within five business days. You may not be the person who submits the form. You are the person who makes sure your provider knows, with enough detail, immediately.
Do not agree to leave it out because it will 'look bad'. Looking bad is not the test. Harm is the test. If you are pressured to delay or soften a reportable incident, report that pressure as well.

steps.title: After the incident
paragraphs: Investigation asks what happened and why the controls failed, not who to blame first. Root cause might be a missing plan, a broken aid, a roster, or a practice everyone had got used to. Workers involved need support, including after a frightening shift. A debrief is not a disciplinary meeting.

The point of the register is improvement. If the same incident type keeps appearing, the plan, the training, or the environment has to change. Closing the file without a change means you expect it to happen again.

title: Quality of Support for Leaders
description: How leaders keep support safe and honest all year: what good practice looks like, how to read your own records, and how to fix gaps while they still matter to the person.
standards: Governance and Operational Management; Quality Management; all Core Module outcomes

steps.title: What good support looks like
paragraphs: A quality review checks whether people are actually receiving safe, respectful support, not whether a folder looks busy. It follows the registration groups you deliver. First, someone reads your documents. Then they talk with workers and participants and visit the service. What workers and participants say is part of the review, because they are the ones who know if the support is real.

Someone independent may read your documents and then talk with workers and participants. Leaders need a rough sense of that timeline so the service is not scrambling to look ready. The useful habit is keeping practice and records honest all year. A fortnight of rewriting documents does not change what happened to the person last Tuesday.
points: A review is about whether support is real
Workers and participants know if it is
Rewriting documents at the last minute does not change what happened

steps.title: The support people should receive
paragraphs: The Core Module describes ordinary good support: rights, governance, provision of supports, the environment, and feedback. Extra modules apply when you deliver high intensity supports, behaviour support, supported independent living, early childhood supports, specialist support coordination, or specialist disability accommodation. You only need the modules that match the support you actually provide.

Standards are revised, and the date they take effect matters. Teach workers the current practice. A procedure from three versions ago, still in the folder, will be what people follow if you have not replaced it. Know which version is live.
points: Standards describe the support, not a folder
Use the modules that match the support you deliver

steps.title: Records that show the support
paragraphs: A policy says what you intend. A procedure says how a worker does it. A record says what happened for a particular person on a particular day. All three have to agree. A beautiful policy that nobody follows is a finding about the support, not about the stationery.

Reviewers talk to workers and participants because a register cannot show whether someone was treated with dignity. 'Not met' means the practice or the record does not show the outcome for the person. A training register is one piece of that picture. It shows who was taught. It does not, on its own, show they support people well. Competence is what happens on the shift.

steps.title: Checking the service yourself
paragraphs: Check yourselves against the outcomes before anyone else does. Read a sample of participant files and worker files. Ask: can I see what this person wanted, what support they received, and what happened when something went wrong? If the file cannot answer that, the support may not be happening.

Write the gaps down: what is missing, whose life it affects, who will fix it, and by when. A gap register no one reads is a diary. A gap you fix while the person is still with you is the point of looking.

steps.title: Fixing what you find
paragraphs: A minor gap is a problem that is real but limited. A major gap is a problem that is widespread or that puts people at serious risk. Both get fixed. The difference is urgency and how widely you look for the same problem.

A corrective action says what will change in the work, who is responsible, and when you will check it worked. 'Retrain staff' is not an action unless you also change the thing that made the safe practice hard. Follow up. If the same gap is still there, the action failed, and the person is still living with it.

title: Person-Centred Emergency and Disaster Management
description: Workers know the provider's emergency and disaster plan and each participant's personal emergency plan, and can keep critical supports going during floods, fires, storms, heatwaves, outages and pandemics.
standards: Emergency and Disaster Management (added 2021); Continuity of Supports

steps.title: Obligations
paragraphs: You need to know how this provider keeps people safe in an emergency, and how this participant's support continues when the usual day falls apart. Continuity means medication, meals, personal care, and essential equipment do not stop because the power is out or the road is closed.
Read the provider plan and the person's own emergency plan before the season they apply to, not during the fire. If you cannot find the plan, say so on an ordinary Tuesday.

steps.title: Who is most at risk
paragraphs: People who depend on power for a ventilator, a feeding pump, a pressure mattress, or a wheelchair charger are at immediate risk in an outage. So is anyone whose medication needs a fridge, or who cannot miss a dose.

Mobility, sensory, and cognitive needs change an evacuation. A person who cannot hear an alarm, who will not leave a familiar room, or who cannot use stairs needs a plan written for them. Isolation makes it worse. Someone who lives alone, or who cannot use a phone, needs a check built into the communication tree, not a hope that they will call you.

steps.title: Personal emergency plans

steps.title: During an event
paragraphs: Use the communication tree. One person does not text thirty others in a panic. Know who you call, and what you report: where you are, who is with you, what support is at risk.

Tell emergency services about power-dependent equipment and anyone who cannot self-evacuate. Follow their instructions. Do not improvise a trip to a worker's house as the plan.

title: Risk Management for Support Workers
description: Give workers a practical way to spot, assess and manage risk on every shift, and to balance safety with the participant's right to take risks.
standards: Risk Management; Safe Environment; Independence and informed choice (dignity of risk)

steps.title: Risk in support settings
paragraphs: Risk on a shift can be environmental (a wet floor, a dog, a dark street), clinical (choking, seizure, a pressure injury), behavioural (distress that puts someone in danger), community (traffic, crowds, other people), or about your own safety (working alone, violence). You hold more than one in your head at once.

A risk register is the organisation's list of known risks and how they are controlled. A participant risk assessment is about this person. Read both before you invent your own rules. If the day does not match the paper, you assess again, and you tell someone.
points: Environmental, clinical, behavioural, community, worker safety

steps.title: Assessing
paragraphs: Likelihood is how probable the harm is. Consequence is how bad it is if it happens. A rare event that would kill someone still matters. A frequent event that causes small harm also matters, because it keeps happening. You do not need a spreadsheet on the doorstep to use the idea.

Dynamic risk assessment is what you do when the situation changes mid-shift. They are more unsteady than yesterday. The usual worker is not here. The footpath is blocked. You pause, you think about harm, and you change the plan. You do not push on because the outing was booked.
points: Dynamic risk assessment during a shift

steps.title: Controlling
paragraphs: Controls work best at the top of the list. Eliminate the hazard if you can. Substitute a safer way. Isolate people from the hazard. Change the equipment or the environment. Change how the task is done. Protective equipment is the last layer, not the first thing you reach for.

Working alone and working in the community remove the easy controls. You need a way to get help, an agreed check-in, and permission to leave. A risk you cannot control with what you have in front of you is a risk you stop and escalate.
points: Hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, isolate, engineer, administrate, PPE

steps.title: Dignity of risk
paragraphs: The participant has the right to choose a life that includes risk. Your discomfort is not the measure. A relationship, a meal, a walk without you hovering, a decision you think is unwise — these can be theirs.

Have the conversation. Say the risk in words they can understand, ask what they want, and agree what would make it safer without taking it over. Write that down. Escalate when serious harm is likely and you cannot reduce it another way: tell your supervisor, and follow the plan. Do not quietly ban the activity because it would be easier.

title: Safeguarding Oversight: A Guide for Board Members
description: Directors and board members understand their responsibilities for quality and safeguarding, and what to ask for so problems reach the board before the regulator.
standards: Governance and Operational Management (governing body responsibilities); Risk Management; Incident Management

steps.title: Board obligations
paragraphs: Board members are responsible for the people the organisation supports, not only for the finances. Key personnel have to be suitable. Governance in the Practice Standards means the board knows whether supports are safe, and acts when they are not.

Some changes must be told to the NDIS Commission: changes in key personnel, and events that affect the provider's suitability. A board that hears about a banning order or a death from the newspaper has already failed the people in the service. Ask to be told, and set up the path so you are.

steps.title: Reading the data

title: Working Through Conflict
description: Practical tools for conflict with colleagues, families and participants that stop small disagreements becoming complaints or incidents.
standards: Human Resource Management; Feedback and Complaints Management

steps.title: Understanding conflict
paragraphs: Conflict in support work usually comes from rosters, different ideas about how to support someone, and families who are frightened or exhausted. It is ordinary. It becomes dangerous when it is ignored and people start undermining the plan, or taking it out on the participant.

Escalation has stages. A disagreement, then a grudge, then a refusal to hand over, then a complaint or an incident. You intervene at the disagreement. You do not wait for the explosion and call it unexpected.
points: Sources in support work: rosters, approaches, families

steps.title: In the moment
paragraphs: Lower your volume and slow down. Give space. Standing over someone in a bathroom is not a negotiation. Name the problem, not the person. 'The handover did not include the seizure' rather than 'You never communicate'.

A time-out is a pause so everyone can think, not a punishment. Agree to come back at a set time. Do not use a time-out to avoid the conversation forever, and do not walk out mid-support and leave a participant unsafe.

steps.title: Resolving
paragraphs: Positions are what people demand. Interests are why. 'I want the morning shift' might mean 'I need to pick my child up' or 'I do not feel safe in that house at night'. Ask why. You can often meet the interest without giving the exact demand.
Agree the next step in concrete words, including who will tell the participant if it affects them. Then follow up. An agreement nobody checks becomes the next conflict, with less trust.

steps.title: Escalating

title: Writing Progress Notes and Keeping Records
description: How to write progress notes that tell the next worker what happened, what the person chose, and how they responded, in plain factual language.
standards: Information Management; Provision of Supports: Support planning and Responsive support provision; NDIS claiming evidence

steps.title: Purpose
paragraphs: A progress note keeps the person's support continuous. The next worker should know what happened, what the person chose, and what to pick up. That is the purpose. A note that exists only to prove a service was billed has already missed the person.
Notes are also a legal record of what you did. Write them so they are true. Truth is what protects the person and you. A polished story that did not happen protects nobody.
points: A true record of the support the person received

title: Positive Behaviour Support in Practice
description: Workers understand that behaviour communicates a need, can implement a behaviour support plan as written, and use proactive strategies so restrictive practices are needed less.
standards: Supplementary module: Implementing Behaviour Support Plans; NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018; Responsive support provision
requirement_status: Explicitly required for workers implementing behaviour support plans

steps.title: Understanding behaviour
paragraphs: Behaviour is communication. It tells you something about pain, fear, sensory load, boredom, a wish to escape a demand, or a wish for contact. You look for the message before you look for a consequence.

The function is the need it meets: escape from a task, attention, a tangible thing, or sensory input. Setting events are the background, such as poor sleep, pain, or a noisy morning. Triggers are the moment it starts. If you only record the behaviour and not what came before, the plan cannot change.

steps.title: The PBS approach

A plan that only says what to do when they are distressed has missed the point. Proactive strategies change the environment, the demand, or the communication so a crisis is less likely.

The practitioner assesses and writes the plan with the person and with the people who will use it. Your role is to follow it as written and to report what actually happens. You do not invent a new consequence on a hard shift and call it the plan.

steps.title: Implementing

title: Understanding Restrictive Practices
description: The Commission's stated top priority is reducing and eliminating restrictive practices. Every worker must recognise all five regulated types, including the ones that hide in daily routines, and know what to do when one is used without authorisation.
standards: NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018; Implementing Behaviour Support Plans; state authorisation processes

steps.title: The five types
paragraphs: There are five regulated restrictive practices. Seclusion confines someone alone so they cannot leave. Chemical restraint is medication used to control behaviour rather than to treat a diagnosed condition, and some PRN is in that category. Mechanical restraint is a device used to restrict movement in order to control behaviour. Physical restraint is using your body to restrict their movement. Environmental restraint restricts access to a place or a thing: a locked door, fridge, cupboard, or gate, when the purpose is control.

The same lock, medicine, or hold can be ordinary care in one situation and a restrictive practice in another. The difference is the purpose, and whether the person can freely stop it. Learn to see the five in daily routines, not only in a crisis.
points: Environmental restraint: locked doors, fridges, cupboards, gates

steps.title: Hidden restrictive practices

Practices hide behind 'for their safety' and behind withholding a possession, an outing, or a cigarette until someone complies. If the person cannot freely end it, question it. A kind motive does not change what it is.

title: Supported Independent Living: Practice Standards for Workers
description: How supported independent living works inside a shared home: each person's plan and privacy, house-level risks, and records that show how that person actually lives.

steps.title: The SIL standards
paragraphs: Supported independent living is the support to live in a home, not the building. It sits inside registration because people were harmed in houses where nobody outside was responsible for the standard of their life.

You need the parts that change a shift: whose plan you follow, which skills you must have before a task, and which 'house rules' are actually rights restrictions. Follow each person's plan. Do not invent a blanket rule to make the house easier to run.

steps.title: Individual within shared
paragraphs: Each person has their own plan, preferences, and routines. The house does not get one lifestyle because the roster prefers it. Privacy means their bedroom, conversations that are not held about them in the kitchen, and personal care out of sight of housemates.

A rule about shared noise can be fair. A rule that stops visitors, locks one person's food, or sets a shower time for staff convenience is not a house rule. It may be a restrictive practice, and it is a rights issue either way.

steps.title: House-level risk
paragraphs: People who live together can harm each other. Conflict and abuse between residents are incidents. Watch for fear, injuries, missing belongings, and one person controlling another's food, money, or room.

Locking everyone's cupboards, or using everyone's PRN to keep the house quiet, is not individual support. Money is recorded per person. On overnight shifts you still respond if someone is unsafe. Waiting until morning because you were the sleepover is not a response.

title: Child Safe Principles
description: Workers understand the ten National Principles, their mandatory reporting obligations in their state, and how grooming and abuse are prevented and reported.

steps.title: The principles
paragraphs: The National Principles for Child Safe Organisations say children are safe when the organisation listens to them, staff are suitable and trained, risks are known, and complaints are acted on. States add their own child safe standards. You follow the ones that apply where you work.

A Working With Children Check is required where the law says so. A clearance is not proof someone is safe. It is one screen. You still watch practice, and you still report concerns. A check does not replace your judgement on a shift.

title: Cover, Catch, Clean: Cough Etiquette in Disability Care
description: How coughs and sneezes spread infection, and how to cover, catch, and clean so people you support are protected.
standards: Safe Environment: infection prevention and control (respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette named in the Standards)

steps.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: Coughs and sneezes spread viruses in droplets, and some infections also travel in smaller aerosols that hang in the air. In a car, a bathroom, or a close personal-care task, you are in that space with the person.
Many people you support are more likely to become seriously unwell from a respiratory infection. Your habits protect them. Staying home when you are sick is part of the same protection.

steps.title: Cover, catch, clean
paragraphs: Cover a cough or sneeze with a tissue, or with the inside of your elbow if you have no tissue. Catch it. Do not use an open hand you then put on a bench, a hoist, or someone's arm.

The tissue goes in a bin, then you clean your hands. If you are symptomatic and still in a setting where you should not be, a mask reduces what you spread, but the right step is usually to be off the shift. Offer the person the same tools: tissues, a bin, and help to clean their hands if they want it.

title: COVID-19 and Infection Prevention: A Guide for Disability Support Workers
description: Respiratory virus management in support settings, including outbreak protocols, so the provider can respond to COVID-19, influenza and RSV seasons.
standards: Safe Environment: infection prevention and control

steps.title: Spread and risk
paragraphs: Respiratory viruses spread in droplets from coughs and sneezes, in smaller aerosols in shared air, and from surfaces people then touch. A home, a van, and a shared house are all places this happens.

Some participants are at higher risk of severe illness: older people, people with respiratory or immune conditions, and people who cannot avoid close contact because they need personal care. Their plan, not a general rule of thumb, tells you what extra precautions they need.

steps.title: Precautions
paragraphs: Standard precautions stay in place: clean hands, respiratory hygiene, the right protective equipment, and safe waste. Transmission-based precautions add masks, eye protection, or gowns when the illness or the task requires them. Follow the current instruction for that person and that illness. Do not invent a lower standard because you are 'used to them'.

Ventilation reduces what hangs in the air. Open a window when you can, and do not sit in a closed car with someone who is coughing if the plan says otherwise. Masks are worn properly, changed when wet, and thrown away. They are not worn under the chin.
