steps.title: Outbreak procedures
paragraphs: An outbreak is more than one person unwell in a way that suggests the same infection is spreading, in a house or a team. You notice it. You do not decide it is 'just a cold going around' and keep rotating staff through the house.

Isolation and cohorting mean unwell people are supported with as little mixing as possible, and staff movement is limited if that is the instruction. Notify the person your process names, and follow public health directions that apply. Those directions outrank a preference to keep the usual roster.

title: Food Safety for Support Workers
description: Safe food handling in participants' kitchens and group homes.
standards: Safe Environment; Mealtime Management; Food Standards Code

steps.title: Foodborne illness
paragraphs: Foodborne illness comes from bacteria, viruses, and toxins in food that was undercooked, left out, or contaminated. The person may not be sick until hours later, so the cause is easy to miss.
Some people become dangerously dehydrated or unwell from a bout that someone else would shake off. Follow their plan, and do not serve food you would not trust yourself. When in doubt, throw it out.

steps.title: Temperature and time
paragraphs: Bacteria grow fastest between 5 and 60 degrees. That is the danger zone. Hot food stays hot, cold food stays cold, and food does not sit on a bench while you do another task.

Cool leftovers quickly, reheat them until they are steaming hot, and respect use-by dates. A sniff is not a test. If the person has a texture-modified meal, the safety rules still apply. You do not leave a thickened drink in a warm room all afternoon.

steps.title: In practice
paragraphs: Participant kitchens are not commercial kitchens, and they are still places people get sick. Look at the fridge, the dates, and the cloth that wipes everything. Shopping and transport: cold food stays cold on the way home. Do not leave it in a hot car while you do another errand.

Clean as you go. A bench used for raw chicken is not then used for a sandwich. If you support someone to cook, build the safe step into the task — washing hands, checking the date — rather than doing it silently and calling it their independence.

title: Infection Prevention and Control for Disability Support Workers
description: How infection spreads and how to stop it on an ordinary shift: hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, protective equipment, cleaning, and what to do when several people are unwell.
audience: All staff (with support worker practical content)
standards: Safe Environment: infection prevention and control, including refresher training (Practice Standards amendment 2021)

steps.title: Chain of infection
paragraphs: Infection needs a chain: a germ, a place it lives, a way out, a way it travels, a way in, and a person it can infect. Break any link and the infection does not travel. You break it with clean hands, with covering coughs, with handling waste safely, with cleaning, and by not working when you are infectious.
The chain is the same in a home, a van, and a centre. You do not need to know the name of the germ to interrupt it.
points: Agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry, host

You do not scale these down because you know the person, or because the shift is short. The precautions are the support.

steps.title: Hand hygiene
paragraphs: The five moments are: before touching a person, before a clean task, after body fluid, after touching the person, and after touching their surroundings. These are the times that protect them, not a wash at the start and end of the shift only.

Use alcohol rub when hands are not visibly dirty. Use soap and water when they are dirty, after the toilet, and after body fluids that rub does not handle well. Gloves are not a substitute. You clean your hands when the gloves come off.

steps.title: PPE
paragraphs: Gloves, gowns or aprons, masks, and eye protection each do a different job. Choose what the task needs. Gloves for fluids and personal care. A gown if your clothes may be splashed. A mask and eye protection if fluid may hit your face.

Put on and take off in the order you were taught, so you do not contaminate your face on the way out. Equipment fits, and it is single use unless it is specifically reusable and you know how it is cleaned. A mask under the chin is not worn.

steps.title: Cleaning
paragraphs: Cleaning removes dirt. Disinfecting kills germs that cleaning leaves behind. You clean first, then disinfect when the procedure says to, and you leave the product for the contact time on the label.

Shared equipment — hoists, wheelchairs, blood pressure cuffs, vehicles — is cleaned between people. Laundry soiled with body fluid is bagged where it is, not shaken through the house, and washed as the provider directs.

steps.title: Outbreaks
paragraphs: Signs of an outbreak are more than one person unwell with a similar illness, in a house or a team, close together in time. New coughs, vomiting, or diarrhoea in several people is a reason to tell someone the same day.

Notification follows your process and any public health instruction. Transmission-based precautions are the extra steps for that illness: the mask, the gown, the limit on who comes and goes. You do not decide the outbreak is over because you are tired of the precautions.

title: Manual Handling: Aids and Equipment Support
description: Safe use of hoists, slide sheets, wheelchairs, walking aids and transfer equipment.
standards: Safe Environment; WHS hazardous manual tasks; Assistive technology use

steps.title: Before use
paragraphs: Before you use a hoist or a sling, check the service tag and the load limit. Out of date or overloaded equipment is how people get dropped. The sling has to be the right type, the right size, and the loops the plan names. A sling from another house is not 'close enough'.
The person's manual handling plan says which equipment, how many workers, and what they can do themselves. Read it. If the equipment does not match the plan, you do not invent a lift while you wait.

steps.title: Hoists

steps.title: Slide sheets and boards
paragraphs: A slide sheet reduces friction so you can reposition someone up or across the bed without dragging their skin or your back. The sheet is under them properly, you have the number of workers the plan says, and you agree the count before you move.

A transfer board bridges two surfaces at a similar height for a person who can assist. It is not a slide from a high bed to a low chair. If the gap, the height, or the person's ability does not match what you were taught, stop.

title: Manual Handling: Mobility Support
description: Supporting people to walk, stand, sit and transfer with the least assistance needed and without injury to either person.
standards: Safe Environment; WHS hazardous manual tasks

steps.title: Assess first
paragraphs: Read the manual handling plan, then look at the person today. Pain, fatigue, new shoes or no shoes, a wet floor, or a day when they are much less steady changes the support. Yesterday's easy walk can be today's fall.
Ask them how they are and watch them sit before you ask them to stand. If the plan and the person in front of you disagree, the safer assessment wins, and you record why.

title: Manual Handling: Safe Support Practices
description: The foundation module: body mechanics, risk assessment and the principles that apply across every manual task.
standards: Safe Environment; WHS hazardous manual tasks

steps.title: Injury
paragraphs: Your spine is injured by bending, twisting, and lifting at the same time, and by doing that in small amounts all year. Cumulative strain does not feel like an accident. It feels like a back that is a bit worse every month, until a small task finishes it.
Care work has high rates of musculoskeletal injury. The techniques exist because workers were hurt, and because participants were dropped. Using them is part of being able to keep supporting people.

steps.title: Roles and authority
paragraphs: There is a difference between prompting someone to take their own medication, assisting them, and administering it. Your role, your training, and the state rules decide which of those you may do. The medication authority or treatment sheet is the instruction. Your memory is not.

This course is the theory. Being signed off as competent to assist or administer is separate. Until you have that sign-off for this task, you do not do it. Scope is not expanded because the usual worker is away.

steps.title: The rights
paragraphs: The rights of medication support are the checks that stop the wrong thing happening: the right person, medicine, dose, time, route, and the right to refuse, plus the documentation and the reason you are giving it. Whatever list of eight your provider uses, you do every check, every time.

Check against the chart, not against what you gave yesterday. Identify the person the way the procedure says, even if you know them. Similar names and webster packs are how errors happen between people who live together.

steps.title: Storage
paragraphs: Medication is stored as the procedure says, usually locked, away from heat, and separate from other people's medicines. Refrigerated items stay in the fridge that is used for them, at the right temperature, not in a door that swings warm all day.

Schedule 8 medicines have extra recording. You follow that register exactly. Disposal of unwanted medicine goes back to a pharmacy or the stream your provider uses. It does not go in the kitchen bin or down the sink.

steps.title: When things go wrong
paragraphs: Errors and near misses are reported the same shift. A missed dose, a double dose, or the wrong person. Say so immediately. Waiting to see if they 'seem fine' wastes the window for advice.

A person may refuse medication. That can be an informed choice. You do not hide it in food, and you do not coerce them. You record the refusal and tell the person the plan names. An adverse reaction or anaphylaxis is an emergency: follow the action plan, call for help, and use the adrenaline device if that is what the plan says and you are trained to do it.

steps.title: Chemical restraint
paragraphs: A medicine given to control behaviour, rather than to treat the condition it was prescribed for, can be a chemical restraint. PRN used because someone is distressed, loud, or 'difficult' is the common case. The behaviour support plan says whether that medicine is authorised as a restrictive practice and what must be tried first.

You do not give it early, give an extra dose, or give it because the house is short-staffed. If it is not authorised, you do not give it for behaviour. You report the request. Authorised use is recorded so it can be reviewed and reduced.

paragraphs: Waste is separated so the right thing is treated safely. General waste, recycling, clinical waste, sharps, pharmaceutical waste, and hazardous waste are not the same bin. Colour and labelling tell you which is which in that house. Learn them before you need them.
If you do not know, ask. Putting clinical waste in recycling, or tablets in the household bin, creates a risk for the person who handles it next.

title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
description: Selecting, fitting, wearing, removing and disposing of PPE without contaminating yourself or the participant.
standards: Safe Environment: infection prevention and control (PPE named in the Standards); WHS

steps.title: Selecting
paragraphs: Choose protective equipment from the risk in front of you, not from habit. Gloves when you will touch fluid or broken skin. A gown or apron when your clothes may be contaminated. A mask when there is a respiratory risk or splash to the mouth. Eye protection when fluid may hit your face. A respirator when the instruction is a respirator, not a surgical mask.
More equipment is not always safer. Gloves worn for the entire shift, touching door handles and then a sandwich, spread contamination. Take them off between tasks.
points: Gloves, gowns, aprons, masks, respirators, eyewear

title: Supporting Safe Mealtimes
description: Choking and aspiration are leading causes of preventable death for NDIS participants. Workers follow mealtime management plans, prepare texture-modified food and fluids, and position and monitor safely.
standards: Safe Environment: Mealtime Management (added 2021); High intensity: severe dysphagia where applicable
requirement_status: Explicitly required where mealtime support is provided

steps.title: Dysphagia
paragraphs: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing. Food or drink can go into the airway instead of the stomach. People at higher risk include those with neurological disability, a history of choking, or coughing during meals. The plan will say if this person is one of them.

Signs are coughing during or after a meal, a wet or gurgly voice, throat clearing, food left in the mouth, and repeated chest infections. Silent aspiration has few signs. That is why you follow the plan even when the meal 'looks fine'.
points: Signs: coughing, wet voice, chest infections

steps.title: Mealtime plans
paragraphs: A mealtime management plan is written by a qualified practitioner, often a speech pathologist, with the person. It says texture, thickness of fluids, position, pace, equipment, and what to do if they choke. You do not write one yourself from experience.

Follow it every meal, including snacks and cups of tea. Ask for a review when swallowing changes: more coughing, a new chest infection, weight loss, or refusal. A plan from two years ago may be dangerous if their swallow has changed.

steps.title: Safe support
paragraphs: The person sits upright, as the plan describes, for the meal and for the time afterwards it specifies. Feeding someone who is reclined is how aspiration happens. Pace the meal. Watch fatigue. A tired swallow is a less safe swallow.

Reduce distractions if the plan says they need to focus. Oral care matters because leftover food and poor mouth care lead to chest infections. Support teeth and mouth cleaning as part of the mealtime, not as an optional extra.

title: The First Line of Defence: Hand Hygiene Essentials
description: The single most effective infection control measure, taught as a short standalone module for induction and refresh.
standards: Safe Environment: infection prevention and control (hand hygiene named in the Standards)

steps.title: Five moments
paragraphs: Clean your hands before you touch a participant, so you do not bring in what was on the last surface. Clean them before a clean or aseptic task, such as a wound or a catheter. Clean them after body fluid exposure, even if you wore gloves.

Clean them after touching the person, and after touching their surroundings: the bed rail, the wheelchair, the bench. The five moments are the practice. A wash when you arrive and when you leave misses the moments that matter.

steps.title: Technique
paragraphs: Soap and water takes 40 to 60 seconds, all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, then dry with a clean towel. Alcohol rub takes 20 to 30 seconds, until the hands are dry. Wet hands are not finished hands.

Soap and water is required when hands are visibly dirty, after the toilet, and when the procedure says rub is not enough. If the product is not there, get it. Skipping because the bottle is empty is an infection decision.

title: Work Health and Safety for Leaders
description: Leaders understand their legal duties, including psychosocial risk, and can run the provider's WHS system for a dispersed workforce in homes and the community.
standards: Model WHS laws: officer due diligence, PCBU duties; Safe Environment; Risk Management

steps.title: Duties
paragraphs: A PCBU is the business that must keep workers and others safe, so far as reasonably practicable. Officers, including directors, must exercise due diligence: understand the risks, make sure resources and processes exist, and make sure those processes are used. Workers must take care and follow the reasonable instruction.

Due diligence is active. Asking for the incident reports, asking whether manual handling equipment is in date, and acting when it is not. Penalties apply when duties are breached, including after someone is hurt. The legal duty and the duty to the person are the same work.

steps.title: Hazards in disability support
paragraphs: The hazards that hurt workers in this sector are manual handling, occupational violence, psychosocial hazards such as bullying and traumatic shifts, and working alone in houses and cars. They are predictable. A leader who is surprised by them has not looked.

Controls have to work in other people's homes, not only in a centre with a store room. That means equipment in the house, a way to get help at night, and rosters that do not leave one worker to do a two-person task.

title: Work Health and Safety for Support Workers
description: Worker duties and practical safety for the realities of the job: other people's homes, cars, community settings, working alone, and occupational violence.

steps.title: Duties
paragraphs: You take reasonable care of your own health and safety, and of others who are affected by what you do. That includes the participant. You follow the reasonable safety instruction, and you cooperate with the procedures.

You may refuse work you reasonably believe is unsafe, and you are protected from being punished for that. Refusing is saying what is unsafe and asking for it to be fixed. It is not walking off and leaving someone without essential support and without telling anyone.

steps.title: Hazards
paragraphs: Manual handling, slips, trips, and falls are the everyday injuries. Chemicals and hot surfaces show up in bathrooms and kitchens: bleach mixed with other cleaners, a kettle, a heater. Do not mix chemicals, and do not leave hot water where someone who cannot move away will be burned.

Dogs, smoking, and hoarding are hazards in people's homes. You do not ignore a dog that has bitten, or a path you cannot walk. Driving is a work task when you drive for support. Fatigue, a phone, and an unsecured wheelchair are driving hazards. Deal with them before you move.

steps.title: Occupational violence
paragraphs: Warning signs are a rising voice, threats, a person cornering you, or a change from their usual distress into something aimed at you. Use the de-escalation in the plan: space, calm voice, a smaller demand. Do not match the volume, and do not block the only exit.

You may leave when you are at risk, once the participant is as safe as you can make them and you have called for help. Then report it. Violence is not 'part of the job' that you absorb. Support after it is part of the response, including for you.

title: Participant Money and Property
description: How to handle a participant's money and belongings only as they have authorised, record every transaction, and notice financial abuse.
audience: Support workers; office and finance staff
standards: Safe Environment: Participant Money and Property; Code of Conduct (integrity); financial abuse prevention

steps.title: Rules
paragraphs: You handle a participant's money and property only as they, or their proper authority, have agreed, and only for the purpose agreed. You do not become their unofficial banker.

You do not know their PIN, you do not store their card in your wallet, and you do not use their online banking. Gifts and borrowing either way are boundary breaches. 'They insisted' does not make it theirs to give if the relationship is one of dependence.

steps.title: Financial abuse
paragraphs: Signs include missing money, a person suddenly unable to pay for things they used to buy, a new 'friend' who takes them to the bank, or a family member who speaks for them about every purchase while they look afraid.

Family and informal supports are sometimes the source, not the protection. You do not need proof. You record what you saw and report it through the safeguarding path. Do not confront the person you suspect, and do not warn them that you are going to report.

title: Work Health and Safety for Office and Administrative Staff
description: Added because WHS duties cover office, reception, finance and rostering staff as much as support workers. Ergonomics, office hazards, psychosocial risk and emergencies.
standards: Model WHS laws; Safe Environment

steps.title: Duties
paragraphs: Office, reception, finance, and rostering work is still work. You take reasonable care of yourself and of anyone affected by what you do, including participants whose plans and rosters you handle. You report hazards rather than working around them.

Consultation means you are asked about changes that affect safety, and you speak up. A roster you build that leaves one worker to do a two-person lift is a safety decision, even though you made it at a desk.

steps.title: Workstations
paragraphs: Set the chair so your feet are supported and your shoulders are relaxed. The screen is at about eye level, the keyboard close enough that you are not reaching. Take breaks from sitting. Pain that arrives every afternoon is information, not a badge of effort.

Working from home does not remove the duty. You still need a setup that does not injure you, and a way to raise a hazard. A laptop on a couch for a full day is a hazard you report, not a perk you endure.

title: Cyber Security Awareness
description: Added because the provider holds participant health information and worker identity documents, and most breaches start with a person. Phishing, passwords, devices, and what to do when something goes wrong.
standards: Information Management; Privacy Act 1988; Notifiable Data Breaches scheme; Australian Cyber Security Centre Essential Eight (awareness level)

steps.title: Threats
paragraphs: Phishing and smishing are fake emails and texts that want a password, a payment, or a click. Invoice and payroll fraud asks you to change bank details. A manager who 'urgently' wants gift cards or a quiet transfer is a classic impersonation. Ransomware locks systems and often starts with one click.

Slow down when a message is urgent, secret, or slightly wrong. Check through a second channel you already trust, not through the number or link in the message. Participant information and worker identity documents are what these attacks are after.

title: Respect at Work
description: Employers now have a positive duty to prevent sexual harassment, sex-based harassment and hostile workplaces. This course covers every worker's role, including with participants and families as sources of harassment.
standards: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 positive duty; Fair Work Act; state anti-discrimination law; Human Resource Management

steps.title: Definitions
paragraphs: Sexual harassment is an unwelcome sexual advance, request, or conduct that a reasonable person would expect to offend, humiliate, or intimidate. It includes comments, images, jokes, and touching. Sex-based harassment is demeaning conduct because of someone's sex, even when it is not 'sexual'.

Discrimination is less favourable treatment because of a protected attribute. Victimisation is punishing someone for complaining. A hostile workplace environment is one where that conduct is allowed to be the culture. Any of these can happen in an office, a group chat, or a participant's home.

steps.title: In support settings
paragraphs: Harassment can come from participants and families, not only from colleagues. You still do not have to accept sexual comments, exposure that is targeted at you, or being touched. The person's disability does not make the behaviour your job to absorb. It does change how the response is planned.

Balance their rights with your safety. The plan should say how this is handled: what you say, when you leave, who you tell. Do not invent a restrictive practice to manage it, and do not ignore it. Online harassment and roster-based harassment — shifts used as punishment, explicit messages — are the same conduct. Screenshot and report.

steps.title: The positive duty

title: Fraud, Conflicts of Interest and Ethical Conduct
description: Added for the office and leadership layer. Claims fraud, kickbacks, conflicts of interest in referrals and support coordination, and gifts and benefits.
standards: Code of Conduct (integrity, honesty, transparency); Governance and Operational Management; NDIS fraud provisions; support coordination conflict of interest guidance

steps.title: Fraud and claiming
paragraphs: Claiming for a support that was not delivered is fraud. So is claiming a longer shift than happened, or a more expensive support than was provided. Over-servicing and up-coding take a participant's budget for something they did not receive.

A participant's NDIS number is not a tool you share so someone else can claim, and it is not something you use out of curiosity. If you are asked to sign a timesheet that is not true, you refuse and you tell someone outside that request.

steps.title: Conflicts of interest
paragraphs: A conflict is when your interest, or your organisation's, could sway a decision that should be the participant's. Referring them to a related provider, or a support coordinator steering them toward the in-house service, is the common case.

The conflict is declared before they choose, other options are offered where they exist, and the choice is recorded. Plan managers and coordinators have the same duty. A register that is never updated is not a declaration.

title: Complex Bowel Care
description: Theory for supporting participants who need bowel care beyond routine assistance, including stoma care, suppositories and enemas, and digital stimulation, under a health practitioner's plan.

steps.title: Anatomy and conditions
paragraphs: The bowel stores and moves stool. Nerves, muscles, fluid, and routine all affect it. A neurogenic bowel, common after spinal injury and in some neurological conditions, does not get the usual signals. Constipation is hard, infrequent stool. Impaction is a blockage of hard stool. Both can make someone very unwell, and in a person with a spinal injury they can trigger autonomic dysreflexia.
You are learning the theory so you understand the plan. You do not diagnose, and you do not change the routine because yesterday was different. The plan is the instruction.

steps.title: Emergencies
paragraphs: Autonomic dysreflexia is a dangerous rise in blood pressure in some people with spinal cord injury. Signs include a pounding headache, sweating, flushing, a blocked nose, and goosebumps above the injury. A bowel problem can cause it. Sit them up if that is the emergency plan, find and relieve the cause only as you are trained, and call for emergency help. Do not lie them flat and wait.
Bleeding, severe pain, or no result when the plan expected one are reasons to stop and contact the person named in the plan. You do not repeat the procedure to 'make it work'.

title: Enteral Feeding and Management
description: Theory for PEG, PEJ and nasogastric feeding: preparing feeds, administering bolus and pump feeds, medication via tube, site care and troubleshooting.
standards: Supplementary module: High Intensity Daily Personal Activities; NDIS High Intensity Support Skill Descriptors
requirement_status: Explicitly required for workers delivering this support; practical competency sign-off by a qualified health practitioner required

steps.title: Types and plans
paragraphs: A PEG goes into the stomach through the abdominal wall. A PEJ goes further, into the jejunum. A nasogastric tube goes through the nose into the stomach and is usually shorter term. They are not interchangeable. The feeding plan says which this person has, what formula, what rate or volume, and what to do if it will not flow.

You follow that plan. You do not give a different feed, a different rate, or food by mouth because they seem hungry, unless the plan says oral intake is allowed. This course is theory. Practical sign-off is separate.

steps.title: Feeding
paragraphs: A bolus is a volume given over a short time. A pump gives the feed at a set rate. Use the method, the volume, and the rate on the plan. Do not speed a pump up to finish before the end of your shift.

Position them upright as the plan says, and keep them upright for the time it specifies, so the feed does not come back and enter the airway. Flush the tube with the amount and the type of water the plan names, before and after, so it does not block.

steps.title: Medication via tube

steps.title: Site care

Granulation tissue is the extra moist tissue that can grow around the site. The plan says how it is managed. You do not cut it or treat it with something from the bathroom cupboard.
Report changes the same day. A site that looks worse than yesterday is not something you 'keep an eye on' until the end of the week.

steps.title: Problems
paragraphs: A blocked tube is managed with the flush and the steps in the plan. Do not force a syringe, and do not poke the tube with an object. A dislodged tube is an emergency of a different kind. Do not try to push it back in. Cover the site as taught and get help immediately. A nasogastric tube that may have moved is not used until placement is confirmed the way the plan requires.

Aspiration signs include coughing, distress, a wet voice, or a change in breathing during or after a feed. Stop the feed and follow the emergency steps. Call 000 when they are in distress, when the tube is dislodged and you cannot reach the clinical contact, or whenever the plan says to.

description: Extends Supporting Safe Mealtimes (SE-14) for participants with severe dysphagia: strict IDDSI compliance, positioning, oral care and choking response.

steps.title: Severe dysphagia
paragraphs: Severe dysphagia means the swallow is unsafe for ordinary food and fluid. The mechanism is poor coordination or sensation, so food or drink enters the airway. Silent aspiration is when that happens without a cough. You will not always see it.

Repeated chest infections can be aspiration pneumonia. That is why the texture, the position, and the pace are not preferences. They are how this person breathes safely. This course builds on safe mealtimes. It does not replace the speech pathologist's plan or your practical sign-off.

steps.title: IDDSI in detail
paragraphs: The flow test checks drink thickness. The fork and spoon tests check food. Use the test for the level on the plan, every time the texture could have changed: a new batch, a drink that sat, a meal that was reheated.

Thickener is added as the plan and the product say. Stirring by eye is how drinks end up too thin. Too thin aspirates. The wrong texture of food can choke. If you cannot get the test to pass, do not serve it.

steps.title: At the table
paragraphs: Position them upright, stable, and supported, as the plan shows, before any food or fluid. Keep them upright afterwards for the time specified. A bolus that is too big, or a pace that is too fast, overwhelms the swallow. Use the spoon and the cues in the plan.

Fatigue makes the swallow worse. A long meal, a recline, or a conversation that distracts them can be the risk. Stop when the plan says to stop, even if there is food left. Offer the rest the way the plan allows, later.

title: Ventilation Support
description: Theory for supporting participants who use invasive or non-invasive ventilation: equipment, monitoring, alarms, and emergency response.
standards: Supplementary module: High Intensity Daily Personal Activities; NDIS High Intensity Support Skill Descriptors

steps.title: Ventilation
paragraphs: Invasive ventilation uses a tube into the airway, such as a tracheostomy. Non-invasive ventilation uses a mask or similar interface. Both support breathing. The settings — pressures, rates, oxygen — are prescribed by a clinician. You do not turn a dial because the alarm is annoying or because they 'seem to want more air'.
This course is theory. You do not support ventilation unless you have been signed off for this person and this equipment.

steps.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: Signs of distress include a change in breathing, colour, sweating, restlessness, drowsiness, and the person saying they cannot breathe. Trust those signs over a machine that looks normal, and trust a machine alarm over a wish that it is a false one.

Oxygen saturation is monitored only as prescribed, with the device and the target in the plan. You do not add oxygen, and you do not chase a number by changing ventilator settings. You follow the response the plan gives for that reading, and you call when it says to call.

title: Tracheostomy Management
description: Theory for tracheostomy care: suctioning, stoma and tube care, humidification, and emergency management of blockage or dislodgement.

steps.title: Tracheostomy
paragraphs: A tracheostomy is an opening into the windpipe so a person can breathe, or so secretions can be cleared. The tube type — cuffed or uncuffed — changes how they breathe and whether they can speak. A speaking valve is used only as the plan allows. You do not put a valve on a cuff that is inflated unless the plan says that combination is safe.
Why this person has the tube, and which type, is in the plan. You do not change tubes or sizes. Theory here is not the practical sign-off.

steps.title: Suctioning
paragraphs: Suctioning clears secretions the person cannot clear. Indications are in the plan: the sound, the distress, the visible secretions. Suctioning because it is 'due' when they are clear can harm. Not suctioning when they are obstructed also harms.

Technique, depth, and how long you suction are set by the plan and by the competency you were signed off for. Deeper and longer is not better. It can injure and it can drop their oxygen. If you are not signed off, you do not suction. You call someone who is.

description: Theory for indwelling, suprapubic and intermittent catheters: drainage systems, hygiene, emptying and changing bags, and recognising infection and blockage.

steps.title: Types
paragraphs: An indwelling urethral catheter stays in the bladder through the urethra. A suprapubic catheter enters through the abdomen. Intermittent catheterisation drains and is removed. They have different care and different risks. The plan says which this person has and who is signed off to change or insert it.
You do not insert or change a catheter because this course explained the types. Insertion is a signed-off skill. Daily care is what the plan authorises you to do.

steps.title: Wounds

If the wound does not match the description in the plan — deeper, wetter, a new smell — stop and get the review. Do not keep applying yesterday's dressing to a wound that has changed.

steps.title: Epilepsy
paragraphs: Seizures are not all the same. Some are convulsive. Some are a blank stare, a strange movement, or a change in awareness. The person's plan names their seizure types. Learn those, not a generic picture.

Triggers may include missed medication, illness, missed sleep, stress, flashing light, or missed meals. They are individual. SUDEP is sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. It is why seizures are taken seriously, why plans exist, and why you do not leave someone alone in the recovery position and walk off.

steps.title: Seizure first aid
paragraphs: Time the seizure from the start. Protect them from injury: something soft under the head, hazards moved away. Do not hold them down and do not put anything in the mouth. When the convulsion stops, the recovery position helps breathing, if that is what you were taught and they are breathing.

Call 000 when the plan says to, when you do not know them, when the seizure is longer than the plan's limit, when a second seizure starts, when they are injured, pregnant, or not breathing normally, or when you are unsure. Stay until they are fully recovered or help has taken over.

steps.title: Midazolam

description: Recognise asthma symptoms, follow the participant's asthma action plan, and give asthma first aid.

steps.title: Asthma
paragraphs: Asthma narrows the airways and fills them with mucus, so breathing out becomes hard. A trigger — a virus, smoke, exercise, pollen, a cold house — can start it. This person's triggers are in their action plan.

You cannot see how tight an airway is from across the room at the start. Learn their early signs: cough, wheeze, saying they are tight, waking at night. The plan is more useful than a general impression.

steps.title: First aid
paragraphs: Sit them upright. Do not lie them down. Follow the national first aid steps you were taught: four puffs of reliever, one puff at a time, with four breaths after each puff, wait four minutes, and repeat if they are not better. Use a spacer if that is what the plan and the training say.

If they are not improving, or they are severe from the start, call 000 and keep giving the reliever as the first aid steps say. Stay with them. An asthma attack that is 'a bit better' can still worsen in the car on the way to somewhere other than hospital.

title: Acquired Brain Injury
description: Understand the effects of ABI on thinking, behaviour, communication and fatigue, and adapt supports.

steps.title: ABI
paragraphs: Acquired brain injury happens after birth, from trauma, stroke, hypoxia, infection, or other causes. Which part of the brain was injured changes the effect: movement, speech, memory, impulse, vision, or personality. Two people with an ABI are not the same support.
It is often invisible. Someone may walk and talk and still be unable to plan, remember, or control an impulse. Do not treat a good conversation as proof they can manage the whole task alone.

steps.title: Cognitive effects
paragraphs: Memory problems mean you do not rely on 'I told them this morning'. Write it down, show it, and repeat without irritation. Attention problems mean one instruction at a time, in a quieter space.

Executive function is starting, sequencing, and stopping. They may know the steps and still not begin. Fatigue is neurological, not laziness. A person can be capable at 9 and unable at 2. Build the day around that, rather than pushing through and calling the result behaviour.

steps.title: Behaviour and emotion
paragraphs: Disinhibition can look like swearing, sexual comments, or saying the quiet part out loud. It is an injury effect, not a personality you punish. You respond calmly, redirect, and do not shame them in front of others.

Irritability may come from fatigue, noise, or too many demands. Reduced insight means they may not see the risk you see. You still involve them in decisions. You do not take over their life because insight is patchy. You adjust the support and explain the risk in the moment.

steps.title: Strategies
paragraphs: Routine reduces the load on memory and planning. Keep the order of the day predictable, and warn them before a change. External memory aids — a phone alarm, a whiteboard, a list they helped write — are the support. Your memory is not the system.

Pace activities. Rest is part of the plan, not a reward. Family and identity matter. They had a life before the injury. Ask what still matters, and do not speak about them as if the injury is the whole person.

steps.title: Autism
paragraphs: Autism is a difference in how a person senses, communicates, and thinks. It is a spectrum of traits, not a line from mild to severe, and it is an identity many people claim with pride. Language follows the person: many prefer 'autistic person'. Ask.

Co-occurring conditions are common, including anxiety, epilepsy, and ADHD. Do not explain every need as 'the autism'. Read the plan for this person. Another autistic person you supported is not the template.

steps.title: Sensory
paragraphs: Hypersensitivity means sound, light, touch, smell, or taste is intense or painful. Hyposensitivity means they may not register pain, temperature, or body position the way you expect. Both can be true in the same person, for different senses.

Change the environment: lower the noise, dim the light, warn before touch, offer the clothing they can bear. Stimming — rocking, flapping, humming — is often regulation. You do not stop it because it looks odd. You only intervene if they are about to be hurt.

steps.title: Communication
paragraphs: Some people use speech, some use a device, pictures, or behaviour. Literal language means sarcasm and hints fail. Say what you mean. Processing time means you ask, then wait. Repeating louder is not waiting.

Masking is when they hide autistic traits to get through a social situation. It is exhausting and it can look like they are 'fine' until they are not. Do not praise them for masking, and do not require eye contact. Communication is successful when they understood you and you understood them, not when they looked at your eyes.

steps.title: Distress
paragraphs: A meltdown is an overload response. It can look like shouting, crying, or hitting. A shutdown is overload that goes quiet: still, unable to speak, withdrawn. Neither is a tantrum you discipline, and neither is solved by more demands.

Prevention is the sensory and communication work earlier in the day. In the moment, reduce input, reduce language, keep them safe, and follow the plan. Do not restrain them to stop the meltdown. Restraint makes overload worse and it may be a restrictive practice.

steps.title: Harmful practices
paragraphs: Compliance-based programs that train a person to obey, to sit still, or to perform 'quiet hands' teach them to ignore their own distress. That is harmful. Forced eye contact is harmful. Stopping a stim that is not hurting anyone is harmful.

Restrictive practices are not autism strategies. They are regulated, last resort, and authorised, or they do not happen. If a program, a school, or a colleague asks you to hold someone down or lock a door to make them comply, you refuse and you report it.

title: Supporting Someone with Bipolar Disorder
description: Recognise mood episodes, support recovery-oriented practice, and respond to risk in mania and depression.
standards: Person-centred supports; Responsive support provision; psychosocial disability

steps.title: Bipolar disorder
paragraphs: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of depression and episodes of elevated mood. Types differ in how high the mood goes and how the episodes are patterned. Mania is a marked high: little sleep, racing speech, grand plans, risk-taking. Hypomania is a milder high that can still wreck money, relationships, and judgement. Depression is the low: slowed, hopeless, sometimes suicidal.

The recovery model means the person leads the life they want, with support, including between episodes. You are not treating the illness. You are supporting the person through the day, using their plan.

steps.title: Risk

title: Supporting Someone with PTSD
description: Extends Trauma Informed Support (RR-11) with the specific features of PTSD and complex PTSD.
standards: Person-centred supports; Responsive support provision; psychosocial disability

steps.title: PTSD
paragraphs: PTSD can follow trauma. Symptom clusters include reliving the event, avoiding reminders, negative changes in thoughts and mood, and being constantly on guard. Complex PTSD can also include difficulties with emotion, self-worth, and relationships, often after prolonged trauma.

It is common among people with disability, including people who lived in institutions or were harmed by people who were meant to care for them. You may be supporting someone for whom a uniform, a bathroom, or a raised voice is a reminder. This course sits alongside trauma-informed support. It does not make you their therapist.

steps.title: Recognising episodes
paragraphs: A flashback is the person re-experiencing the trauma now. They may not be fully in the room with you. Dissociation is a disconnect: blank, unreachable, or 'not here'. Hyperarousal is jumpiness, anger, scanning for danger. Avoidance is refusing places, topics, or care that remind them.

Do not grab them, shout, or demand they 'come back'. Use their name, orient them gently to where they are, and follow the plan. What looks like refusal of personal care may be avoidance of a trigger. Force is the worst response.

steps.title: Support

title: Supporting Someone with Schizophrenia
description: Understand psychosis and negative symptoms, support recovery, and respond to relapse and risk.
standards: Person-centred supports; Responsive support provision; psychosocial disability

steps.title: Schizophrenia
paragraphs: Schizophrenia affects thinking, perception, emotion, and motivation. Symptoms can include delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, and what are called negative symptoms: flat expression, little speech, withdrawal, difficulty starting. The course varies. Many people live well with treatment and support between episodes.
Stigma is part of what you are there to not add. Do not joke about 'being psycho', do not assume they are dangerous, and do not talk about them as their diagnosis. Read the plan for this person.

steps.title: Responding to psychosis
paragraphs: If they are describing a delusion or a hallucination, you do not argue the content and you do not pretend you can see or hear it. You validate the feeling. 'That sounds frightening' is useful. 'That is not real' is a fight you will not win, and it can wreck trust.

Keep the scene safe. Reduce stimulation. Give space. Use the de-escalation in the plan. If they are at risk, or someone else is, follow the crisis steps and call for help. Stay calm. A room full of workers closing in is not calming.

steps.title: Recovery support
paragraphs: Routine, sleep, meals, and something meaningful in the day are the support. Negative symptoms can look like laziness. They are not. Offer, wait, and do the step with them rather than taking the day over or abandoning them to a dark room.

Physical health matters. Some medicines affect weight, movement, and heart risk. Notice the side effects the plan names — stiffness, restlessness, thirst — and report them. You do not suggest they stop the medicine because of a side effect. You get that information to the prescriber through the proper path.

title: Introduction to Coercive Control
description: Recognise coercive control in participants' relationships, including by carers and family, and know how to respond and refer.
standards: Violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; state coercive control laws

steps.title: Coercive control
paragraphs: Coercive control is a pattern of domination: isolation, monitoring, humiliation, control of money, threats, and rules, not only physical hits. One incident may look small. The pattern is the harm. The person may defend the controller and still be unsafe.

Laws differ by state. Some recognise coercive control as an offence. You do not need to know the charge to take the pattern seriously. Your organisation's procedure says how you record and refer. Follow it.

steps.title: Disability and risk
paragraphs: The perpetrator may be the carer, the partner, a parent, or a worker. Dependence makes leaving harder. The person may rely on the controller for personal care, communication, or a place to live. They may not be believed because of their disability.

Control can run through the support itself: speaking for them, withholding the wheelchair or the communication device, cancelling workers they trust, managing all the money, refusing to leave the room during personal care. Watch who is afraid of whom.

steps.title: Responding

Use the referral pathway: domestic violence services that can work with people with disability, police when there is immediate danger, and your provider's safeguarding lead. Offer the referral. Do not force them to leave on your timetable. Do not promise you can keep them safe by yourself.

title: Understanding the Types and Signs of Abuse
description: Five-minute refresher from RR-01. Five types of abuse with two indicators each; a 60-second recap video and a matching activity. Match the indicator to the abuse type; Which two signs suggest financial abuse; True or false: neglect can be unintentional
standards: Refresher bite for RR-01

steps.title: Understanding the Types and Signs of Abuse
paragraphs: Abuse is harm done to a person. Physical abuse includes hitting, pushing, rough handling, and force used to get a task done. Sexual abuse is any sexual act, exposure, or comment without free consent, including where the person cannot consent. Emotional and psychological abuse is threats, humiliation, isolation, or constant criticism that wears someone down. Financial abuse and exploitation is taking money, property, or benefits, or pressuring someone to hand them over.

Neglect is care that does not happen. Active neglect is refusing care you know the person needs. Passive neglect is not noticing that they have not eaten, been changed, or had their medication. Discrimination and systemic abuse is when rules, routines, or attitudes treat a person as less, or shut them out of ordinary life. You notice harm through the body (injuries, pain, weight loss), through behaviour (fear, withdrawal, a new sexualised act), and through the place (no food, a locked room, missing belongings). This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

title: How to Respond to Abuse
description: Five-minute refresher from RR-01. The four steps of a first response: safety, listen, do not investigate, record. What is your first priority; Which of these should you never say; Order the four response steps
standards: Refresher bite for RR-01

steps.title: How to Respond to Abuse
paragraphs: If someone tells you they have been hurt, listen and believe them enough to act. You do not interview them, ask leading questions, or make them repeat the story for each new person. Your job is safety, not the investigation. Meet immediate medical needs first. If they are injured, bleeding, or in pain, get health care. If they are unsafe with a person who is still there, separate them.

Say you are glad they told you, that they are not in trouble, and that you will get help. Do not promise secrecy. You will have to tell the people whose job it is to protect them. Leave clothing, bedding, and the place as they are when you can do that without leaving the person unsafe. Do not confront the person they named. Confrontation can silence them, destroy evidence, and put you both at risk. Write down the words they used, as soon as you can, and report. This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

title: How to Report Abuse
description: Five-minute refresher from RR-01. Internal pathway, reportable incident categories and the 24-hour rule. Who do you report to first; Which incidents go to the Commission within 24 hours; True or false: your supervisor decides whether to notify the Commission
standards: Refresher bite for RR-01

steps.title: How to Report Abuse
paragraphs: Tell your provider through the incident pathway the same shift, not at the end of the week. Say what you saw or were told, who was there, and what you did. Do not wait to be sure. The people who assess the report decide what happens next. If a child is involved, police and the child-protection report in your state may be required as well as the internal report. Do that immediately. Do not agree to 'keep it in the house'.

Some events are reportable to the NDIS Commission. Death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact, and sexual misconduct are reported within 24 hours. You tell your provider so they can make that notification. You are protected when you report in good faith. Retaliation for raising a safety concern is itself a breach. If you fear reprisal, you can also complain directly to the Commission. This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

steps.title: Understanding Reportable Incidents
paragraphs: Some incidents must be notified to the NDIS Commission. Death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact, and sexual misconduct are notified within 24 hours. Unauthorised use of a restrictive practice is notified within five business days. You may not be the person who submits the form. You are the person who makes sure your provider knows, with enough detail, immediately.

Do not agree to leave it out because it will 'look bad'. Looking bad is not the test. Harm is the test. If you are pressured to delay or soften a reportable incident, report that pressure as well. This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

description: Five-minute refresher from GO-07. What a factual incident report contains and when it is due. Which sentence is factual; By when must the report be lodged; What is missing from this sample report

steps.title: Reporting an Incident
paragraphs: Write facts. What you saw, what you heard, what you did, and the time. 'He was aggressive' is an opinion. 'He hit the table with his fist and said he wanted to leave' is a fact. Leave out diagnoses and guesses about motive.

Write it the same day, in the incident system, not only in a progress note. The register is how patterns are seen. A fall every Tuesday that lives in six different notebooks is invisible. This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

title: Understanding Chemical Restraint
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-03. PRN medication for behaviour, authorisation, reporting. When is PRN a chemical restraint; Where must it be authorised; How often is use reported
standards: Refresher bite for PS-03

steps.title: Understanding Chemical Restraint
paragraphs: Chemical restraint is medication given to control behaviour, not to treat a diagnosed condition. That includes a PRN given because someone is distressed, loud, or refusing a task. The same medicine can be treatment in one situation and a restraint in another. The behaviour support plan says which is which.

You do not give it because the shift is hard or because it worked yesterday. If it is authorised, you follow the plan's conditions: when, how much, and what else you try first. If it is not in the plan, you do not give it, and you report the request. Any use is recorded so the practitioner can see whether the practice is reducing.

title: Understanding Emotional Regulation
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-01. Co-regulation, early signs, environment changes. What is co-regulation; Which is an early sign; Which environment change helps
standards: Refresher bite for PS-01

steps.title: Understanding Emotional Regulation
paragraphs: Emotional regulation is a person's ability to feel a strong emotion and get back to a state where they can take part. Many people you support are still building that skill, or they lose it when they are in pain, frightened, hungry, or overloaded. Behaviour in that moment is communication, not a choice to ruin the shift.

You help by lowering demands, keeping your voice slow, and offering the strategy in their plan: space, a known person, a sensory item, a change of room. You do not lecture, restrain, or threaten a consequence while they are flooded. Afterwards, when they are calm, you can talk about what happened if they want to. You record what led up to it and what helped.

title: Understanding Environmental Restraint
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-03. Locked doors, fridges, gates, removing items; blanket rules. Is a locked front door at night a restraint; Who does a locked fridge affect; What makes it authorised
standards: Refresher bite for PS-03

steps.title: Understanding Environmental Restraint
paragraphs: Environmental restraint restricts a person's free access to places or things they would otherwise use. Locked doors, gates, cupboards, fridges, and devices can all be environmental restraint when they are used to control a person, even if the house calls them 'just how we do things'. A lock for everyone's ordinary safety, such as a pool gate, is different from a lock that stops one person leaving their room.

If a restriction is in the behaviour support plan and authorised, you use only that restriction, for the time and purpose it names, and you record it. You do not add a lock because it makes the shift easier. If you find a restriction that is not in the plan, you stop using it where it is safe to do so, and you report it.

title: Understanding Mechanical Restraint
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-03. Belts, rails, splints and the therapeutic exception. When is a bed rail a restraint; What is the therapeutic exception; Who must authorise
standards: Refresher bite for PS-03

steps.title: Understanding Mechanical Restraint
paragraphs: Mechanical restraint is a device used to restrict movement, such as a strap, belt, splint, or table that a person cannot undo, when the purpose is to control behaviour. A device the person uses for posture or safety, and can release, or that a therapist has prescribed for a physical reason, is not automatically a restraint. The plan tells you which is which.

You use an authorised device only as the plan describes, you check skin and comfort, and you take it off as soon as the plan says to. You never tie, wedge, or strap someone in place because there are not enough staff. Unauthorised use is reported.

title: Understanding Physical Restraint
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-03. Holding, blocking, guiding; what is and is not restraint. Is blocking a doorway with your body a restraint; Is a brief hand on the arm to prevent a trip a restraint; What must happen after unauthorised use
standards: Refresher bite for PS-03

steps.title: Understanding Physical Restraint
paragraphs: Physical restraint is using your body to stop a person moving, when the purpose is to control behaviour. Holding someone's hands down, sitting on them, or pinning them to a chair are physical restraint. Guiding a hand during personal care, with their agreement, is not. The difference is force and purpose.

You do not use physical restraint to finish a task, win an argument, or keep to the clock. If a plan authorises a specific hold as a last resort to prevent serious harm, you use only that hold, for the shortest time, and you release as soon as the harm has passed. You record it the same day. Any other hold is reported.

title: Understanding Seclusion
description: Five-minute refresher from PS-03. Sole confinement, time-outs and why they are regulated. Is a 'quiet room' with a closed door seclusion; Can seclusion be used on a child; What must be recorded
standards: Refresher bite for PS-03

steps.title: Understanding Seclusion
paragraphs: Seclusion is putting a person alone in a room or area and stopping them from leaving. Shutting a door and holding it, or telling someone they cannot come out until they calm down, is seclusion even if you stay nearby and call it 'time away'. A person choosing to be in their room, with the door able to open, is not seclusion.

Seclusion is a regulated restrictive practice. You use it only when it is in the behaviour support plan, authorised, and the last resort to prevent serious harm. You stay responsible for their safety the whole time, you end it as soon as you can, and you record the start, the finish, and what you tried first. If it is not authorised, you do not do it, and you report anyone who does.
points: why they are regulated. Is a 'quiet room' with a closed door seclusion; Can seclusion be used on a child; What must be recorded

steps.title: Sharps Safety
paragraphs: Used sharps go straight into an approved sharps container, at the place you used them. The container is rigid, labelled, and not filled past the line. It is not a drink bottle, a plastic bag, or the kitchen bin.

Never recap a needle, and never bend or snap it. Most needle-stick injuries happen when someone tries to make a used needle 'safer' by hand. Clinical waste (material soaked with blood or body fluid) is a different stream from ordinary household rubbish. If you are unsure which bag to use, ask before you throw it in with the recycling or the kitchen waste. This is a short return to the idea. The full course goes further.

description: Five-minute refresher from SE-06. Who is suitable, positioning, safety. Which participant is not suitable; Where are the feet; What if they cannot hold on
standards: Refresher bite for SE-06

steps.title: Stand Hoist Transfer
paragraphs: A stand hoist supports a person who can bear some weight and follow the steps, to move between sitting surfaces. It is not a shortcut for someone who cannot stand. The manual handling plan says whether this person uses a stand hoist, which sling, and whether you need a second worker.

Check the service tag and the load limit before you start. Fit the sling as the plan shows, explain each step, and stop if the person is in pain or their feet are not taking weight. You do not swap in a full-body sling, a different loop, or a one-person attempt because the second worker is late. If the hoist fails, tag it out and report it. Do not invent another way to lift.

steps.title: Incident Reporting Checkpoint
paragraphs: An incident is an act, an omission, an event, or a circumstance that harmed a participant or a worker, or could have. Dropping someone, missing a medication, a participant hurting someone, abuse, a fall, a missing person. Near misses count. The hoist sling that nearly failed is how you prevent the next one. If you only record injuries, you only learn after someone is hurt. Make people safe and get medical help first. First aid, an ambulance, separating people, turning off a hazard. Comfort the person in a way they can use. Do not interview them for the perfect note while they are injured or terrified.

title: Infection Prevention and Control Checkpoint
description: A short return to hand hygiene, protective equipment, and respiratory hygiene so you can still use them on shift.
standards: Refresher for SE-05, SE-13, SE-15, SE-02

steps.title: Infection Prevention and Control Checkpoint
paragraphs: Infection needs a chain: a germ, a place it lives, a way out, a way it travels, a way in, and a person it can infect. Break any link and the infection does not travel. You break it with clean hands, with covering coughs, with handling waste safely, with cleaning, and by not working when you are infectious. Standard precautions are used with every person, whether or not they have a known infection. Hand hygiene. Protective equipment matched to the task. Respiratory hygiene. Safe sharps and waste. Basic aseptic technique when you are doing something that must stay clean, such as a wound or a catheter, as you have been taught.

Choose protective equipment from the risk in front of you, not from habit. Gloves when you will touch fluid or broken skin. A gown or apron when your clothes may be contaminated. A mask when there is a respiratory risk or splash to the mouth. Eye protection when fluid may hit your face. A respirator when the instruction is a respirator, not a surgical mask. Put equipment on in the order you were taught, so the parts that must stay clean stay clean. Take it off in the order that keeps contaminated surfaces away from your face and clothes. The doffing is where people infect themselves. The questions after this check that you can still use the practice.

steps.title: Manual Handling Checkpoint
paragraphs: Before you use a hoist or a sling, check the service tag and the load limit. Out of date or overloaded equipment is how people get dropped. The sling has to be the right type, the right size, and the loops the plan names. A sling from another house is not 'close enough'. A full-body hoist moves someone who cannot stand safely. You explain each step, fit the sling as taught, keep them involved, and move smoothly. Brakes and the path are checked before you raise them.

Read the manual handling plan, then look at the person today. Pain, fatigue, new shoes or no shoes, a wet floor, or a day when they are much less steady changes the support. Yesterday's easy walk can be today's fall. Set their feet, give them time, and cue in the words the plan uses. Do not pull on their arms. Stand close, on their weaker side if that is the instruction, and let them do the work they can do. The questions after this check that you can still use the practice.

title: Human Rights Hub
description: Session material drawn from RR-09, RR-10, RR-07. Not assessed as a competency.
standards: Draws from RR-09, RR-10, RR-07

steps.title: RR-09: Rights and capacity
paragraphs: Every adult is presumed able to make their own decisions. Disability, a guardian, or a hard decision does not cancel that presumption. You start by supporting the decision, not by taking it.

Capacity is decision-specific. A person may decide what to eat and need support to decide about a medical procedure. You do not treat 'has a cognitive disability' as 'cannot decide anything'. The standard you are aiming at is their will and preferences — what they want — not what you believe is in their best interests. Best interests is the old habit of deciding for people.
points: Will and preferences versus best interests

image.alt: Rights and capacity

steps.title: RR-09: Supported versus substitute
paragraphs: Supported decision-making is a range. You explain, you wait, you offer options, you involve a person they trust. Substitute decision-making is someone else deciding in their place. A guardian, an administrator, or a nominee has authority only for the decisions in their order. Read what it actually covers.

A guardian for accommodation does not automatically decide dinner, clothes, or who visits. An administrator manages money, not relationships. If you are unsure, ask to see the order rather than handing the decision to a family member who sounds confident. When the person can decide, they decide, even if a guardian exists for other matters.
points: What a guardian can and cannot decide

image.alt: Supported versus substitute

steps.title: RR-10: Models of disability
paragraphs: The medical model locates the problem in the person's body or mind and tries to fix them. The charity model sees them as someone to be pitied and helped. The social model says people are disabled by barriers: stairs, attitudes, inflexible routines. The human rights model says they are rights-holders, and support exists so they can live on equal terms.

Language follows the model. 'Suffering from', 'wheelchair-bound', and 'non-compliant' put the problem in the person. Talk about the person first, the support they use, and the barrier in front of them. Attitudes show up in small acts: talking to the worker instead of the person, deciding they will not want to come, calling a choice 'behaviour'.
points: Medical, charity, social and human rights models

image.alt: Models of disability

steps.title: RR-10: The rights framework
paragraphs: The UN Convention sets out rights that matter on a shift: equality, accessibility, living independently, privacy, health, and being free from exploitation and abuse. You will not quote article numbers at the door. You will notice when a routine cancels one of those rights.

The NDIS Act principles say people have the same rights as other Australians, and they should be able to exercise choice. The Disability Discrimination Act makes it unlawful to treat someone less favourably because of disability. A provider's convenience is not a defence.
points: UNCRPD articles most relevant to supports

image.alt: The rights framework

steps.title: RR-07: Why active support
paragraphs: Active support means the person takes part in their own life, at whatever level they can, instead of having life done to them. Engagement — doing, choosing, being with people — is what makes a day feel like theirs. Quality of life is that participation, not a tidy house.

The hotel model is the opposite. Workers cook, clean, and decide, and the person waits. It looks efficient and it shrinks someone's skills. Research on active support shows that when staff step back to the right amount of help, people do more and spend less time disengaged. Your job is to enable, not to complete the task fastest.

image.alt: Why active support

steps.title: RR-07: The four essentials
paragraphs: Every moment has potential. Folding one towel, choosing a shirt, or stirring a pot counts. You do not wait for a program called 'activities'. Little and often beats a long session nobody can sustain. Graded assistance is the skill: ask, then instruct, then prompt, then show, then guide physically. You start with the least help that works, and you add help only for the step they cannot do yet.
Choice and control run through all of it. You offer real options, not a pretend choice after you have already decided. If they pick the option that takes longer, that is the support working.
points: Graded assistance: ask, instruct, prompt, show, guide

image.alt: The four essentials

title: Restrictive Practices Hub
description: Session material drawn from PS-03, PS-01. Not assessed as a competency.
standards: Draws from PS-03, PS-01

steps.title: PS-03: The five types
paragraphs: There are five regulated restrictive practices. Seclusion confines someone alone so they cannot leave. Chemical restraint is medication used to control behaviour rather than to treat a diagnosed condition, and some PRN is in that category. Mechanical restraint is a device used to restrict movement in order to control behaviour. Physical restraint is using your body to restrict their movement. Environmental restraint restricts access to a place or a thing: a locked door, fridge, cupboard, or gate, when the purpose is control.

The same lock, medicine, or hold can be ordinary care in one situation and a restrictive practice in another. The difference is the purpose, and whether the person can freely stop it. Learn to see the five in daily routines, not only in a crisis.
points: Environmental restraint: locked doors, fridges, cupboards, gates

image.alt: The five types

steps.title: PS-03: Hidden restrictive practices
paragraphs: A rule that 'applies to everyone' can still restrict the person who cannot leave, cannot open the fridge, or cannot choose. Eating at five can be a shared routine. Locking the cupboard so one person cannot eat is environmental restraint when they cannot consent and cannot get to their own food.

Practices hide behind 'for their safety' and behind withholding a possession, an outing, or a cigarette until someone complies. If the person cannot freely end it, question it. A kind motive does not change what it is.

image.alt: Hidden restrictive practices

steps.title: PS-01: Understanding behaviour
paragraphs: Behaviour is communication. It tells you something about pain, fear, sensory load, boredom, a wish to escape a demand, or a wish for contact. You look for the message before you look for a consequence.

The function is the need it meets: escape from a task, attention, a tangible thing, or sensory input. Setting events are the background, such as poor sleep, pain, or a noisy morning. Triggers are the moment it starts. If you only record the behaviour and not what came before, the plan cannot change.

image.alt: Understanding behaviour

steps.title: PS-01: The PBS approach
paragraphs: Positive behaviour support aims at a life the person wants: relationships, something to do, and control over the day. A plan that only says what to do when they are distressed has missed the point. Proactive strategies change the environment, the demand, or the communication so a crisis is less likely.

The practitioner assesses and writes the plan with the person and with the people who will use it. Your role is to follow it as written and to report what actually happens. You do not invent a new consequence on a hard shift and call it the plan.
points: The practitioner's role and the worker's role

image.alt: The PBS approach

title: Infection Prevention and Control Hub
description: Session material drawn from SE-05, SE-13, SE-15, SE-02, SE-03. Not assessed as a competency.
standards: Draws from SE-05, SE-13, SE-15, SE-02, SE-03

steps.title: SE-05: Chain of infection
paragraphs: Infection needs a chain: a germ, a place it lives, a way out, a way it travels, a way in, and a person it can infect. Break any link and the infection does not travel. You break it with clean hands, with covering coughs, with handling waste safely, with cleaning, and by not working when you are infectious.
The chain is the same in a home, a van, and a centre. You do not need to know the name of the germ to interrupt it.
points: Agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry, host

image.alt: Chain of infection

steps.title: SE-05: Standard precautions
paragraphs: Standard precautions are used with every person, whether or not they have a known infection. Hand hygiene. Protective equipment matched to the task. Respiratory hygiene. Safe sharps and waste. Basic aseptic technique when you are doing something that must stay clean, such as a wound or a catheter, as you have been taught.
You do not scale these down because you know the person, or because the shift is short. The precautions are the support.

image.alt: Standard precautions

steps.title: SE-13: Selecting
paragraphs: Choose protective equipment from the risk in front of you, not from habit. Gloves when you will touch fluid or broken skin. A gown or apron when your clothes may be contaminated. A mask when there is a respiratory risk or splash to the mouth. Eye protection when fluid may hit your face. A respirator when the instruction is a respirator, not a surgical mask.
More equipment is not always safer. Gloves worn for the entire shift, touching door handles and then a sandwich, spread contamination. Take them off between tasks.
points: Gloves, gowns, aprons, masks, respirators, eyewear

image.alt: Selecting

steps.title: SE-13: Donning and doffing
paragraphs: Put equipment on in the order you were taught, so the parts that must stay clean stay clean. Take it off in the order that keeps contaminated surfaces away from your face and clothes. The doffing is where people infect themselves.

Common errors: touching the outside of a glove with a bare hand, pulling a mask down and then back up, and wiping your face with a gloved hand. If you are unsure of the order, stop and follow the poster or ask. Guessing is how the germ gets to your mouth.

image.alt: Donning and doffing

steps.title: SE-15: Five moments
paragraphs: Clean your hands before you touch a participant, so you do not bring in what was on the last surface. Clean them before a clean or aseptic task, such as a wound or a catheter. Clean them after body fluid exposure, even if you wore gloves.

Clean them after touching the person, and after touching their surroundings: the bed rail, the wheelchair, the bench. The five moments are the practice. A wash when you arrive and when you leave misses the moments that matter.

image.alt: Five moments

steps.title: SE-15: Technique
paragraphs: Soap and water takes 40 to 60 seconds, all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, then dry with a clean towel. Alcohol rub takes 20 to 30 seconds, until the hands are dry. Wet hands are not finished hands.

Soap and water is required when hands are visibly dirty, after the toilet, and when the procedure says rub is not enough. If the product is not there, get it. Skipping because the bottle is empty is an infection decision.

image.alt: Technique

steps.title: SE-02: Why it matters
paragraphs: Coughs and sneezes spread viruses in droplets, and some infections also travel in smaller aerosols that hang in the air. In a car, a bathroom, or a close personal-care task, you are in that space with the person.
Many people you support are more likely to become seriously unwell from a respiratory infection. Your habits protect them. Staying home when you are sick is part of the same protection.

image.alt: Why it matters

steps.title: SE-02: Cover, catch, clean
paragraphs: Cover a cough or sneeze with a tissue, or with the inside of your elbow if you have no tissue. Catch it. Do not use an open hand you then put on a bench, a hoist, or someone's arm.

The tissue goes in a bin, then you clean your hands. If you are symptomatic and still in a setting where you should not be, a mask reduces what you spread, but the right step is usually to be off the shift. Offer the person the same tools: tissues, a bin, and help to clean their hands if they want it.

image.alt: Cover, catch, clean

steps.title: SE-03: Spread and risk
paragraphs: Respiratory viruses spread in droplets from coughs and sneezes, in smaller aerosols in shared air, and from surfaces people then touch. A home, a van, and a shared house are all places this happens.

Some participants are at higher risk of severe illness: older people, people with respiratory or immune conditions, and people who cannot avoid close contact because they need personal care. Their plan, not a general rule of thumb, tells you what extra precautions they need.

image.alt: Spread and risk

steps.title: SE-03: Precautions
paragraphs: Standard precautions stay in place: clean hands, respiratory hygiene, the right protective equipment, and safe waste. Transmission-based precautions add masks, eye protection, or gowns when the illness or the task requires them. Follow the current instruction for that person and that illness. Do not invent a lower standard because you are 'used to them'.

Ventilation reduces what hangs in the air. Open a window when you can, and do not sit in a closed car with someone who is coughing if the plan says otherwise. Masks are worn properly, changed when wet, and thrown away. They are not worn under the chin.

image.alt: Precautions
