title: Manual Handling Hub
description: Session material drawn from SE-06, SE-07, SE-08, SE-09, SE-10. Not assessed as a competency.
standards: Draws from SE-06, SE-07, SE-08, SE-09, SE-10

steps.title: SE-06: Before use
paragraphs: Before you use a hoist or a sling, check the service tag and the load limit. Out of date or overloaded equipment is how people get dropped. The sling has to be the right type, the right size, and the loops the plan names. A sling from another house is not 'close enough'.
The person's manual handling plan says which equipment, how many workers, and what they can do themselves. Read it. If the equipment does not match the plan, you do not invent a lift while you wait.
points: Right sling, right size, right loops

image.alt: Before use

steps.title: SE-06: Hoists
paragraphs: A full-body hoist moves someone who cannot stand safely. You explain each step, fit the sling as taught, keep them involved, and move smoothly. Brakes and the path are checked before you raise them.

A stand hoist is only for a person the plan says can bear weight and follow the steps. Two-person tasks stay two-person. If the second worker is not there, the task waits or you get help. You do not do a two-person hoist alone because the shift is short.

image.alt: Hoists

steps.title: SE-07: Assess first
paragraphs: Read the manual handling plan, then look at the person today. Pain, fatigue, new shoes or no shoes, a wet floor, or a day when they are much less steady changes the support. Yesterday's easy walk can be today's fall.
Ask them how they are and watch them sit before you ask them to stand. If the plan and the person in front of you disagree, the safer assessment wins, and you record why.
points: Dynamic assessment: pain, fatigue, footwear, environment

image.alt: Assess first

steps.title: SE-07: Sit-to-stand and walking
paragraphs: Set their feet, give them time, and cue in the words the plan uses. Do not pull on their arms. Stand close, on their weaker side if that is the instruction, and let them do the work they can do.
Belts and walking aids are used only as assessed. A belt is not a handle to haul someone up. Match their pace. Rushing the walk to stay on time is how falls happen.

image.alt: Sit-to-stand and walking

steps.title: SE-08: Set-up
paragraphs: Set the bed, the commode, or the shower chair at a height that lets you work without bending and twisting. Bring what you need before you start so you are not leaving them half-supported while you look for a towel.

Awkward postures — twisting while holding, reaching across a bed, kneeling on a wet floor — are how cumulative injury happens. Change the setup. Do not 'just manage' a bad position because it is quicker.

image.alt: Set-up

steps.title: SE-08: In bed
paragraphs: Rolling and moving someone up the bed uses the sheet or the technique in the plan, with the number of people it names. You explain, you agree a count, and you avoid dragging skin.
If the plan says two people, one person does not do it 'just this once'. Get the second person or change the task. A single-worker drag is an injury to both of you.

image.alt: In bed

steps.title: SE-09: Injury
paragraphs: Your spine is injured by bending, twisting, and lifting at the same time, and by doing that in small amounts all year. Cumulative strain does not feel like an accident. It feels like a back that is a bit worse every month, until a small task finishes it.
Care work has high rates of musculoskeletal injury. The techniques exist because workers were hurt, and because participants were dropped. Using them is part of being able to keep supporting people.

image.alt: Injury

steps.title: SE-09: Principles
paragraphs: Plan the move before you start. Assess the load, the environment, and the person today. Communicate what will happen, and position your feet so you can move without twisting.

Move with your legs and your whole body, not by hinging your back and hauling. If you cannot get close, if you have to twist, or if the person cannot do the part the plan assumes, stop and reset. Force is not a technique.
points: Move with the body, not the back

image.alt: Principles

steps.title: SE-10: Before transfer
paragraphs: Park so the door opens fully and the person is not stepping into traffic. Look at the kerb, the seat height, and the slope. A transfer that worked in a driveway may not work on a camber.
Use the aids the plan names: a swivel cushion, a board, a handle. Do not use a worker's body as the aid because the cushion was left at home. Go back for it, or change the plan for today with help.

image.alt: Before transfer

steps.title: SE-10: Car transfers
paragraphs: The usual pattern is sit first, then bring the legs in, and the reverse to get out. You support and guide. You do not lift a person into a seat by their arms or under their shoulders.

If they cannot do the movement the plan describes, stop. Forcing a transfer into a low car seat is a common way to injure a shoulder, yours or theirs. A different vehicle or a different method is the answer.

image.alt: Car transfers
